items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. Grounding in real world signals To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. Industry specific simulation We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. Automated query generation While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. The six-stage pipeline Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets ! items.content: Content Creation / Rendering Speed Up Image Generation with FLUX 3 Image Klein on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs Nov 06, 2026 By Olivia Stoner , Yiheng Zhang , Chang Liu , Seonghee Lee and Gunjan Mehta Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary FLUX 3 Image Klein Base and its distilled variant combine Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer, and an autoencoder to generate and edit images at high resolution. TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with NVFP4 quantization, fused PrimsTS GEMM kernels, and torch.compile, delivering up to 1.62x faster text-to-image and 1.58x faster image-to-image generation over BF16 on a single B200. Quantized attention options include cuDNN FP8 and VC-Attention FP8; VC-Attention FP8 with a repair budget of 0.005 achieved 1.18x speedups for both Base and distilled models at 2048x2048 with LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151. Sol-Attention sparse attention with τ=1.0 and 12 initial dense steps provided 1.30x faster denoising plus decoding for Base, while 16 dense steps prioritized fidelity at 1.24x. Cache-DiT step caching nearly halved Base latency at both 1024x1024 and 2048x2048, reaching 1.94x speedup at the higher resolution with an LPIPS of 0.033. Multi-GPU scaling with CFG and Ulysses parallelism on eight B200 GPUs reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and from 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled, with denoising speedups of 6.01x and 4.44x. Next Steps Run the FLUX 3 example to execute end-to-end inference with the provided YAML configurations. Explore the TensorRT LLM VisualGen runtime and optimization utilities to understand the optimization APIs. File issues or share results on the TensorRT LLM GitHub to engage with the development team. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more When deploying diffusion models in design tools, image editors, and visual production workflows, developers must account for inference latency. Generating an image requires multiple sequential passes through a model with billions of parameters, and higher resolutions increase attention costs. FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers Base and distilled checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements. This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads. FLUX 3 inference with TensorRT LLM VisualGen FLUX 3 Image Klein combines Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer (DiT) to refine image latents, and an autoencoder to decode latents into images and encode I2I reference inputs. Klein processes text, noisy target-image, and optional reference-image streams independently before combining them through joint attention. TensorRT LLM VisualGen, a dedicated runtime within TensorRT LLM, supported BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 variants at launch. On an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU, NVFP4 delivered up to 1.62x faster T2I and 1.58x faster I2I generation than BF16. Figure 2 compares generation latency, while Figure 1 compares example outputs. The following sections use NVFP4 as the starting point for further optimization. Figure 1 compares outputs at 2048×2048. The summarized T2I prompt describes a kitchen still life; the summarized I2I prompt requests changes to a space scene, including a red gas giant, a silver dragon, and an engraved plaque. T2I · BF16 T2I · NVFP4 I2I · BF16 I2I · NVFP4 Figure 1. BF16 and NVFP4 outputs for T2I and I2I Figure 2. FLUX 3 Image Klein generation latency With NVFP4 as the starting point, VisualGen optimizations turned to denoising, which dominates overall generation time on B200. Accelerating FLUX 3’s DiT is therefore the focus of the following sections. Table 1 shows pipeline latency at 2048×2048 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU using NVFP4, VANILLA attention, and torch.compile. Results are averaged over 10 requests after two warmup requests. Base uses 50 denoising steps with a classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 steps without CFG. Task Model Text + preparation Denoising Decode + postprocess Total Denoising share T2I Base 47 ms 14.24 s 416 ms 14.70 s 96.8% T2I Distilled 24 ms 2.28 s 410 ms 2.71 s 84.0% I2I Base 468 ms 39.40 s 417 ms 40.29 s 97.8% I2I Distilled 407 ms 6.65 s 418 ms 7.48 s 89.0% Table 1. FLUX 3 Image Klein pipeline latency on NVIDIA B200 Optimizing FLUX 3 in TensorRT LLM VisualGen TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates NVFP4 DiT inference with optimized general matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels and epilogue fusion, low-precision and sparse attention, caching, and multi-GPU execution. Unless otherwise noted, the following benchmarks use torch.compile and seed 0. Base uses 50 denoising steps and a CFG scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 denoising steps. NVFP4 inference VisualGen supports BFL’s prequantized NVFP4 DiT checkpoints for FLUX 3 Image Klein and FLUX 3 Image Klein Base . To use these checkpoints, set variant to nvfp4 in pipeline_config : pipeline_config: variant: nvfp4 GEMM kernel optimization TensorRT LLM VisualGen uses FlashInfer’s PrimsTS FP8/NVFP4 GEMM kernels, built with CUTLASS Primitives and Task Scheduling to accelerate quantized inference. Tuned for FLUX 3 tensor shapes and enabled by default, they combine optimized GEMMs with fused epilogues, including GEMM with SwiGLU and query, key, and value (QKV) projections with query/key normalization and rotary position embeddings (RoPE). See FlashInfer PR #5758 for more details. At launch, the pinned NVFP4 PrimsTS kernels delivered 1.02–1.10x faster T2I generation on B200 than the autotuned TensorRT LLM NVFP4 GEMM implementation. Figure 3. T2I latency with PrimsTS and TensorRT LLM GEMMs Quantized and sparse attention Attention is a major bottleneck in high-resolution image generation. In the reported 2048×2048 NVFP4 T2I tests on B200, VANILLA BF16 attention accounted for approximately 60% of DiT GPU kernel time for both Base and distilled Klein. VisualGen supports two approaches to reducing this cost: quantized attention with cuDNN FP8 or VC-Attention FP8, and sparse attention with Sol-Attention . VC-Attention FP8 is a TensorRT LLM variant of the method described in the VC-Attention paper . Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) measures perceptual differences between generated images. In the following comparisons, lower scores indicate greater similarity to the corresponding VANILLA baseline output. Compared with VANILLA BF16 attention, cuDNN FP8 delivered generation speedups of 1.08x for Base and 1.09x for the 16-step distilled Klein. The corresponding LPIPS scores were 0.072 and 0.161. VC-Attention FP8 delivered speedups of 1.18x for Base and 1.16x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151. Figure 4 compares FLUX 3 Image Klein Base NVFP4 outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled. These measurements suggest using VC-Attention FP8 for quantized attention at 2048×2048 on B200. The tested configuration uses a repair budget of ρ=0.005 to select the fraction of tokens with the highest quantization error for residual correction. To use quantized attention, replace attention_config with one of the following configurations: For cuDNN FP8: attention_config: backend: CUDNN quant_attention_config: qk_dtype: fp8 v_dtype: fp8 For VC-Attention FP8: attention_config: backend: TRTLLM quant_attention_config: qk_dtype: fp8 v_dtype: fp8 vc_attention: true vc_repair_budget: 0.005 Tea scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Tea scene · cuDNN FP8 · 1.08x · LPIPS 0.072 Tea scene · VC-Attn FP8 ρ=0.005 · 1.18x · LPIPS 0.086 Cat scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Cat scene · cuDNN FP8 · 1.08x · LPIPS 0.066 Cat scene · VC-Attn FP8 ρ=0.005 · 1.18x · LPIPS 0.049 Figure 4. BF16, cuDNN FP8, and VC-Attention FP8 example outputs Sol-Attention reduces DiT computation with sparsity controlled by τ. The reported tests use the PrimsTS-based general block-sparse attention kernel in TensorRT LLM. Configure Sol-Attention as follows: attention_config: backend: TRTLLM sparse_attention_config: algorithm: sol_attn tau: 1.0 disabled_until_timestep: 0.96 For NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base at 2048×2048 on B200, Sol-Attention with τ=1.0 delivered 1.24x faster denoising plus autoencoder decoding than compiled dense VANILLA with 16 initial dense steps, or 1.30x with 12. These measurements suggest using 16 initial dense steps to prioritize fidelity or 12 to prioritize speed. Higher τ reduced output quality with little additional speedup. Figure 5 compares NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled and τ=1.0. Tea scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Tea scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 16 dense steps · 1.235x · LPIPS 0.075 Tea scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 12 dense steps · 1.297x · LPIPS 0.151 Cat scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Cat scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 16 dense steps · 1.235x · LPIPS 0.116 Cat scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 12 dense steps · 1.297x · LPIPS 0.140 Figure 5. Dense attention and Sol-Attention outputs with 16 or 12 initial dense steps Step caching Cache-DiT reduces FLUX 3 Image Klein inference latency by reusing intermediate transformer outputs across denoising steps without retraining or modifying model weights. A residual-difference threshold controls when cached outputs are reused, so you can adjust the balance between inference speed and output quality. Configure Cache-DiT with your desired parameters: cache_config: cache_backend: cache_dit Fn_compute_blocks: 1 Bn_compute_blocks: 0 max_warmup_steps: 4 max_continuous_cached_steps: 3 residual_diff_threshold: 0.24 At a threshold of 0.24, Cache-DiT nearly halved NVFP4 Base T2I latency at both tested resolutions, with smaller gains for the distilled Klein. At 1024×1024, speedups were 1.97x for Base and 1.26x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.038 and 0.036 against their respective uncached outputs. At 2048×2048, speedups were 1.94x for Base and 1.20x for distilled Klein (Figure 6). Base without Cache-DiT · 1x · LPIPS 0.000 Base with Cache-DiT · 1.94x · LPIPS 0.033 Distilled Klein without Cache-DiT · 1x · LPIPS 0 Distilled Klein with Cache-DiT · 1.20x · LPIPS 0.022 Figure 6. Base and distilled Klein outputs with and without Cache-DiT Multi-GPU inference The VisualGen runtime in TensorRT LLM scales FLUX 3 Image Klein using classifier-free guidance (CFG) and Ulysses sequence parallelism. Base assigns positive/negative branches to separate GPU groups and partitions each branch’s sequence with Ulysses; distilled runs without CFG and uses Ulysses alone. VisualGen handles sequence splitting, distributed attention, and output gathering. For eight-GPU NVFP4 Base inference, use the following configuration: parallel_config: cfg_size: 2 ulysses_size: 4 For the distilled model, set cfg_size: 1 , ulysses_size: 8 , and use the flux-3-image-klein checkpoint. At 2048×2048, scaling from one to eight GPUs on an NVIDIA DGX B200 reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled. Denoising speedups were larger, at 6.01x for Base and 4.44x for distilled Klein, but roughly half of eight-GPU distilled generation time remained outside denoising, limiting end-to-end gains. Figure 7. FLUX 3 Image Klein multi-GPU scaling At smaller resolutions, CUDA Graphs complement parallelism by reducing kernel-launch overhead as work per GPU shrinks. In a separate 1024×1024 NVFP4 experiment on eight B200s with VANILLA attention, adding CUDA Graphs to compilation reduced Base latency from 1.823 to 0.809 seconds (2.25x, CFG across two GPU groups with Ulysses across four GPUs per group) and distilled latency from 0.791 to 0.366 seconds (2.16x, Ulysses across eight GPUs). Enable CUDA Graphs with the following configuration: cuda_graph_config: enable: true FLUX 3 end-to-end performance At 2048×2048, Figure 8 compares end-to-end generation speedups across successive TensorRT LLM VisualGen optimization stages against uncompiled BF16 VANILLA inference. On a single B200, compilation, NVFP4 with PrimsTS GEMMs, Sol-Attention, and Cache-DiT delivered a 3.46x generation speedup for T2I, reducing latency from 22.36 to 6.46 seconds, and a 4.45x speedup for I2I, reducing latency from 54.64 to 12.28 seconds. The 16-step distilled Klein achieved up to 2.34x end-to-end speedups. On a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, compilation, NVFP4 with fused CuTe DSL kernels, and Cache-DiT delivered 1.73-3.25x generation speedups, extending the gains across both platforms. Figures 9 and 10 compare example outputs across optimization stages. Figure 8. Cumulative single-GPU speedups across optimization stages The examples in Figures 9 and 10 were generated on a single B200 GPU. 1. BF16, VANILLA attention · LPIPS 0 2. + torch.compile · LPIPS 0 3. + PrimsTS NVFP4 · LPIPS 0.044 4. + Sol-Attention · LPIPS 0.084 5. + Cache-DiT · LPIPS 0.095 Figure 9. FLUX 3 Image Klein Base T2I outputs across optimization stages The editing prompt requests a weathered appearance for the canoe while preserving its shape, position, and surrounding scene. 1. BF16, VANILLA attention · LPIPS 0 2. + torch.compile · LPIPS 0 3. + PrimsTS NVFP4 · LPIPS 0.031 4. + Sol-Attention · LPIPS 0.029 5. + Cache-DiT · LPIPS 0.045 Figure 10. FLUX 3 Image Klein Base I2I outputs across optimization stages To apply these optimizations to your own workloads, follow the runtime setup, inference commands, and YAML configurations in the following sections for offline generation or online serving. Prerequisites Start the prebuilt TensorRT LLM container with the following command. To build it from the feat/flux3-image-klein branch, follow the FLUX 3 deployment guide . docker run --rm -it --ipc=host --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \ --name tensorrt_llm \ -e TLLM_FMHA_LIBS=+prims_ts \ -e HF_TOKEN=<your_hf_token> \ -v ~/.cache:/root/.cache:rw \ nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:feat-flux3-image-klein-1.4.0a0.dev202610280436 TLLM_FMHA_LIBS=+prims_ts enables the PrimsTS attention kernels VC-Attention requires. The optimizations and results in this post focus on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Get started with TensorRT LLM VisualGen With the runtime environment ready, you can run FLUX 3 offline or serve it through an image generation endpoint. Use the sample YAML configurations in the following sections to apply the optimization settings used for the results reported earlier. These examples do not expand prompts. If you use BFL’s prompt upsampler, run it separately before inference. Reported latencies exclude prompt upsampling. Offline inference Inside the container, run the FLUX 3 example : cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen python models/flux3.py \ --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \ --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml \ --prompt "A small robot tending a rooftop garden at sunrise" \ --height 2048 --width 2048 --seed 0 \ --output_path flux3.png For NVFP4 on Blackwell, add --variant nvfp4 ; use --variant fp8r for row-wise FP8 or omit --variant for BF16. Select black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein for the distilled model. For editing, add an editing prompt and --image /path/to/reference.png ; repeat --image for multiple references. Online serving endpoint From the same container directory, launch the OpenAI-compatible /v1/images/generations endpoint: cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen trtllm-serve black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml Once the server is ready, open a second terminal, enter the running container, and run the client: docker exec -it tensorrt_llm bash python examples/visual_gen/serve/sync_image_gen.py \ --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 \ --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \ --size 2048x2048 \ --prompt "A small robot tending a rooftop garden at sunrise" \ --output flux3-served.png For NVFP4 serving, add pipeline_config: {variant: nvfp4} to the YAML before starting the server; use fp8r for FP8. Optimized single-GPU deployment For 2048×2048 inference on one B200, save the following as configs/ flux3-nvfp4-vc-fp8-1gpu.yaml , which combines NVFP4 weights, torch.compile, and VC-Attention FP8. pipeline_config: variant: nvfp4 torch_compile_config: enable: true compilation_config: resolutions: [[2048, 2048]] num_frames: [1] modes: [t2i, i2i] attention_config: backend: TRTLLM quant_attention_config: qk_dtype: fp8 v_dtype: fp8 vc_attention: true vc_repair_budget: 0.005 For Sol-Attention and Cache-DiT, copy this file to configs/ flux3-nvfp4-sol-cache-1gpu.yaml , replace attention_config , and add cache_config : pipeline_config: variant: nvfp4 torch_compile_config: enable: true compilation_config: resolutions: [[2048, 2048]] num_frames: [1] modes: [t2i, i2i] attention_config: backend: TRTLLM sparse_attention_config: algorithm: sol_attn tau: 1.0 disabled_until_timestep: 0.96 cache_config: cache_backend: cache_dit Fn_compute_blocks: 1 Bn_compute_blocks: 0 max_warmup_steps: 4 max_continuous_cached_steps: 3 residual_diff_threshold: 0.24 The timestep cutoff of 0.96 keeps the first 12 denoising steps dense for 50-step FLUX 3 Image Klein Base and the first four steps dense for 16-step distilled Klein under the packaged α=6.93 schedule. For the 16-dense-step setting recommended above, set disabled_until_timestep: 0.94 . The cutoff specifies a noise level rather than a number of steps. Remove cache_config to use Sol-Attention without Cache-DiT. Set --visual_gen_args in the offline inference or serving commands to the path of your selected YAML file. Set the image size to 2048×2048 to match the performance examples. Conclusion and next steps TensorRT LLM VisualGen supports FLUX 3 Image Klein inference with configurable performance optimizations. NVFP4, fused kernels, compilation, multi-GPU execution, and CUDA Graphs accelerate execution; quantized and sparse attention and caching provide further latency reductions with measurable effects on output quality. Together, they deliver up to 3.46x faster T2I and 4.45x faster I2I generation using a single GPU on an NVIDIA DGX B200, compared with uncompiled BF16 VANILLA inference. TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with NVFP4 quantization, fused PrimsTS GEMM kernels, and torch.compile, delivering up to 1.62x faster text-to-image and 1.58x faster image-to-image generation over BF16 on a single B200. Quantized attention options include cuDNN FP8 and VC-Attention FP8; VC-Attention FP8 with a repair budget of 0.005 achieved 1.18x speedups for both Base and distilled models at 2048x2048 with LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151. Sol-Attention sparse attention with τ=1.0 and 12 initial dense steps provided 1.30x faster denoising plus decoding for Base, while 16 dense steps prioritized fidelity at 1.24x. Cache-DiT step caching nearly halved Base latency at both 1024x1024 and 2048x2048, reaching 1.94x speedup at the higher resolution with an LPIPS of 0.033. Multi-GPU scaling with CFG and Ulysses parallelism on eight B200 GPUs reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and from 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled, with denoising speedups of 6.01x and 4.44x. Next Steps Run the FLUX 3 example to execute end-to-end inference with the provided YAML configurations. Explore the TensorRT LLM VisualGen runtime and optimization utilities to understand the optimization APIs. File issues or share results on the TensorRT LLM GitHub to engage with the development team. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more When deploying diffusion models in design tools, image editors, and visual production workflows, developers must account for inference latency. Generating an image requires multiple sequential passes through a model with billions of parameters, and higher resolutions increase attention costs. FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers Base and distilled checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements. This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads. FLUX 3 inference with TensorRT LLM VisualGen FLUX 3 Image Klein combines Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer (DiT) to refine image latents, and an autoencoder to decode latents into images and encode I2I reference inputs. Klein processes text, noisy target-image, and optional reference-image streams independently before combining them through joint attention. TensorRT LLM VisualGen, a dedicated runtime within TensorRT LLM, supported BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 variants at launch. On an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU, NVFP4 delivered up to 1.62x faster T2I and 1.58x faster I2I generation than BF16. Figure 2 compares generation latency, while Figure 1 compares example outputs. The following sections use NVFP4 as the starting point for further optimization. Figure 1 compares outputs at 2048×2048. The summarized T2I prompt describes a kitchen still life; the summarized I2I prompt requests changes to a space scene, including a red gas giant, a silver dragon, and an engraved plaque. T2I · BF16 T2I · NVFP4 I2I · BF16 I2I · NVFP4 Figure 1. BF16 and NVFP4 outputs for T2I and I2I Figure 2. FLUX 3 Image Klein generation latency With NVFP4 as the starting point, VisualGen optimizations turned to denoising, which dominates overall generation time on B200. Accelerating FLUX 3’s DiT is therefore the focus of the following sections. Table 1 shows pipeline latency at 2048×2048 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU using NVFP4, VANILLA attention, and torch.compile. Results are averaged over 10 requests after two warmup requests. Base uses 50 denoising steps with a classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 steps without CFG. Task Model Text + preparation Denoising Decode + postprocess Total Denoising share T2I Base 47 ms 14.24 s 416 ms 14.70 s 96.8% T2I Distilled 24 ms 2.28 s 410 ms 2.71 s 84.0% I2I Base 468 ms 39.40 s 417 ms 40.29 s 97.8% I2I Distilled 407 ms 6.65 s 418 ms 7.48 s 89.0% Table 1. FLUX 3 Image Klein pipeline latency on NVIDIA B200 Optimizing FLUX 3 in TensorRT LLM VisualGen TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates NVFP4 DiT inference with optimized general matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels and epilogue fusion, low-precision and sparse attention, caching, and multi-GPU execution. Unless otherwise noted, the following benchmarks use torch.compile and seed 0. Base uses 50 denoising steps and a CFG scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 denoising steps. NVFP4 inference VisualGen supports BFL’s prequantized NVFP4 DiT checkpoints for FLUX 3 Image Klein and FLUX 3 Image Klein Base . To use these checkpoints, set variant to nvfp4 in pipeline_config : pipeline_config: variant: nvfp4 GEMM kernel optimization TensorRT LLM VisualGen uses FlashInfer’s PrimsTS FP8/NVFP4 GEMM kernels, built with CUTLASS Primitives and Task Scheduling to accelerate quantized inference. Tuned for FLUX 3 tensor shapes and enabled by default, they combine optimized GEMMs with fused epilogues, including GEMM with SwiGLU and query, key, and value (QKV) projections with query/key normalization and rotary position embeddings (RoPE). See FlashInfer PR #5758 for more details. At launch, the pinned NVFP4 PrimsTS kernels delivered 1.02–1.10x faster T2I generation on B200 than the autotuned TensorRT LLM NVFP4 GEMM implementation. Figure 3. T2I latency with PrimsTS and TensorRT LLM GEMMs Quantized and sparse attention Attention is a major bottleneck in high-resolution image generation. In the reported 2048×2048 NVFP4 T2I tests on B200, VANILLA BF16 attention accounted for approximately 60% of DiT GPU kernel time for both Base and distilled Klein. VisualGen supports two approaches to reducing this cost: quantized attention with cuDNN FP8 or VC-Attention FP8, and sparse attention with Sol-Attention . VC-Attention FP8 is a TensorRT LLM variant of the method described in the VC-Attention paper . Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) measures perceptual differences between generated images. In the following comparisons, lower scores indicate greater similarity to the corresponding VANILLA baseline output. Compared with VANILLA BF16 attention, cuDNN FP8 delivered generation speedups of 1.08x for Base and 1.09x for the 16-step distilled Klein. The corresponding LPIPS scores were 0.072 and 0.161. VC-Attention FP8 delivered speedups of 1.18x for Base and 1.16x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151. Figure 4 compares FLUX 3 Image Klein Base NVFP4 outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled. These measurements suggest using VC-Attention FP8 for quantized attention at 2048×2048 on B200. The tested configuration uses a repair budget of ρ=0.005 to select the fraction of tokens with the highest quantization error for residual correction. To use quantized attention, replace attention_config with one of the following configurations: For cuDNN FP8: attention_config: backend: CUDNN quant_attention_config: qk_dtype: fp8 v_dtype: fp8 For VC-Attention FP8: attention_config: backend: TRTLLM quant_attention_config: qk_dtype: fp8 v_dtype: fp8 vc_attention: true vc_repair_budget: 0.005 Tea scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Tea scene · cuDNN FP8 · 1.08x · LPIPS 0.072 Tea scene · VC-Attn FP8 ρ=0.005 · 1.18x · LPIPS 0.086 Cat scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Cat scene · cuDNN FP8 · 1.08x · LPIPS 0.066 Cat scene · VC-Attn FP8 ρ=0.005 · 1.18x · LPIPS 0.049 Figure 4. BF16, cuDNN FP8, and VC-Attention FP8 example outputs Sol-Attention reduces DiT computation with sparsity controlled by τ. The reported tests use the PrimsTS-based general block-sparse attention kernel in TensorRT LLM. Configure Sol-Attention as follows: attention_config: backend: TRTLLM sparse_attention_config: algorithm: sol_attn tau: 1.0 disabled_until_timestep: 0.96 For NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base at 2048×2048 on B200, Sol-Attention with τ=1.0 delivered 1.24x faster denoising plus autoencoder decoding than compiled dense VANILLA with 16 initial dense steps, or 1.30x with 12. These measurements suggest using 16 initial dense steps to prioritize fidelity or 12 to prioritize speed. Higher τ reduced output quality with little additional speedup. Figure 5 compares NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled and τ=1.0. Tea scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Tea scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 16 dense steps · 1.235x · LPIPS 0.075 Tea scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 12 dense steps · 1.297x · LPIPS 0.151 Cat scene · Dense baseline · 1.000x · LPIPS 0.000 Cat scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 16 dense steps · 1.235x · LPIPS 0.116 Cat scene · Sol-Attn τ=1.0 · 12 dense steps · 1.297x · LPIPS 0.140 Figure 5. Dense attention and Sol-Attention outputs with 16 or 12 initial dense steps Step caching Cache-DiT reduces FLUX 3 Image Klein inference latency by reusing intermediate transformer outputs across denoising steps without retraining or modifying model weights. A residual-difference threshold controls when cached outputs are reused, so you can adjust the balance between inference speed and output quality. Configure Cache-DiT with your desired parameters: cache_config: cache_backend: cache_dit Fn_compute_blocks: 1 Bn_compute_blocks: 0 max_warmup_steps: 4 max_continuous_cached_steps: 3 residual_diff_threshold: 0.24 At a threshold of 0.24, Cache-DiT nearly halved NVFP4 Base T2I latency at both tested resolutions, with smaller gains for the distilled Klein. At 1024×1024, speedups were 1.97x for Base and 1.26x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.038 and 0.036 against their respective uncached outputs. At 2048×2048, speedups were 1.94x for Base and 1.20x for distilled Klein (Figure 6). Base without Cache-DiT · 1x · LPIPS 0.000 Base with Cache-DiT · 1.94x · LPIPS 0.033 Distilled Klein without Cache-DiT · 1x · LPIPS 0 Distilled Klein with Cache-DiT · 1.20x · LPIPS 0.022 Figure 6. Base and distilled Klein outputs with and without Cache-DiT Multi-GPU inference The VisualGen runtime in TensorRT LLM scales FLUX 3 Image Klein using classifier-free guidance (CFG) and Ulysses sequence parallelism. Base assigns positive/negative branches to separate GPU groups and partitions each branch’s sequence with Ulysses; distilled runs without CFG and uses Ulysses alone. VisualGen handles sequence splitting, distributed attention, and output gathering. For eight-GPU NVFP4 Base inference, use the following configuration: parallel_config: cfg_size: 2 ulysses_size: 4 For the distilled model, set cfg_size: 1 , ulysses_size: 8 , and use the flux-3-image-klein checkpoint. At 2048×2048, scaling from one to eight GPUs on an NVIDIA DGX B200 reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled. Denoising speedups were larger, at 6.01x for Base and 4.44x for distilled Klein, but roughly half of eight-GPU distilled generation time remained outside denoising, limiting end-to-end gains. Figure 7. FLUX 3 Image Klein multi-GPU scaling At smaller resolutions, CUDA Graphs complement parallelism by reducing kernel-launch overhead as work per GPU shrinks. In a separate 1024×1024 NVFP4 experiment on eight B200s with VANILLA attention, adding CUDA Graphs to compilation reduced Base latency from 1.823 to 0.809 seconds (2.25x, CFG across two GPU groups with Ulysses across four GPUs per group) and distilled latency from 0.791 to 0.366 seconds (2.16x, Ulysses across eight GPUs). Enable CUDA Graphs with the following configuration: cuda_graph_config: enable: true FLUX 3 end-to-end performance At 2048×2048, Figure 8 compares end-to-end generation speedups across successive TensorRT LLM VisualGen optimization stages against uncompiled BF16 VANILLA inference. On a single B200, compilation, NVFP4 with PrimsTS GEMMs, Sol-Attention, and Cache-DiT delivered a 3.46x generation speedup for T2I, reducing latency from 22.36 to 6.46 seconds, and a 4.45x speedup for I2I, reducing latency from 54.64 to 12.28 seconds. The 16-step distilled Klein achieved up to 2.34x end-to-end speedups. On a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, compilation, NVFP4 with fused CuTe DSL kernels, and Cache-DiT delivered 1.73-3.25x generation speedups, extending the gains across both platforms. Figures 9 and 10 compare example outputs across optimization stages. Figure 8. Cumulative single-GPU speedups across optimization stages The examples in Figures 9 and 10 were generated on a single B200 GPU. 1. BF16, VANILLA attention · LPIPS 0 2. + torch.compile · LPIPS 0 3. + PrimsTS NVFP4 · LPIPS 0.044 4. + Sol-Attention · LPIPS 0.084 5. + Cache-DiT · LPIPS 0.095 Figure 9. FLUX 3 Image Klein Base T2I outputs across optimization stages The editing prompt requests a weathered appearance for the canoe while preserving its shape, position, and surrounding scene. 1. BF16, VANILLA attention · LPIPS 0 2. + torch.compile · LPIPS 0 3. + PrimsTS NVFP4 · LPIPS 0.031 4. + Sol-Attention · LPIPS 0.029 5. + Cache-DiT · LPIPS 0.045 Figure 10. FLUX 3 Image Klein Base I2I outputs across optimization stages To apply these optimizations to your own workloads, follow the runtime setup, inference commands, and YAML configurations in the following sections for offline generation or online serving. Prerequisites Start the prebuilt TensorRT LLM container with the following command. To build it from the feat/flux3-image-klein branch, follow the FLUX 3 deployment guide . docker run --rm -it --ipc=host --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \ --name tensorrt_llm \ -e TLLM_FMHA_LIBS=+prims_ts \ -e HF_TOKEN=<your_hf_token> \ -v ~/.cache:/root/.cache:rw \ nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:feat-flux3-image-klein-1.4.0a0.dev202610280436 TLLM_FMHA_LIBS=+prims_ts enables the PrimsTS attention kernels VC-Attention requires. The optimizations and results in this post focus on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Get started with TensorRT LLM VisualGen With the runtime environment ready, you can run FLUX 3 offline or serve it through an image generation endpoint. Use the sample YAML configurations in the following sections to apply the optimization settings used for the results reported earlier. These examples do not expand prompts. If you use BFL’s prompt upsampler, run it separately before inference. Reported latencies exclude prompt upsampling. Offline inference Inside the container, run the FLUX 3 example : cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen python models/flux3.py \ --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \ --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml \ --prompt "A small robot tending a rooftop garden at sunrise" \ --height 2048 --width 2048 --seed 0 \ --output_path flux3.png For NVFP4 on Blackwell, add --variant nvfp4 ; use --variant fp8r for row-wise FP8 or omit --variant for BF16. Select black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein for the distilled model. For editing, add an editing prompt and --image /path/to/reference.png ; repeat --image for multiple references. Online serving endpoint From the same container directory, launch the OpenAI-compatible /v1/images/generations endpoint: cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen trtllm-serve black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml Once the server is ready, open a second terminal, enter the running container, and run the client: docker exec -it tensorrt_llm bash python examples/visual_gen/serve/sync_image_gen.py \ --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 \ --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \ --size 2048x2048 \ --prompt "A small robot tending a rooftop garden at sunrise" \ --output flux3-served.png For NVFP4 serving, add pipeline_config: {variant: nvfp4} to the YAML before starting the server; use fp8r for FP8. Optimized single-GPU deployment For 2048×2048 inference on one B200, save the following as configs/ flux3-nvfp4-vc-fp8-1gpu.yaml , which combines NVFP4 weights, torch.compile, and VC-Attention FP8. pipeline_config: variant: nvfp4 torch_compile_config: enable: true compilation_config: resolutions: [[2048, 2048]] num_frames: [1] modes: [t2i, i2i] attention_config: backend: TRTLLM quant_attention_config: qk_dtype: fp8 v_dtype: fp8 vc_attention: true vc_repair_budget: 0.005 For Sol-Attention and Cache-DiT, copy this file to configs/ flux3-nvfp4-sol-cache-1gpu.yaml , replace attention_config , and add cache_config : pipeline_config: variant: nvfp4 torch_compile_config: enable: true compilation_config: resolutions: [[2048, 2048]] num_frames: [1] modes: [t2i, i2i] attention_config: backend: TRTLLM sparse_attention_config: algorithm: sol_attn tau: 1.0 disabled_until_timestep: 0.96 cache_config: cache_backend: cache_dit Fn_compute_blocks: 1 Bn_compute_blocks: 0 max_warmup_steps: 4 max_continuous_cached_steps: 3 residual_diff_threshold: 0.24 The timestep cutoff of 0.96 keeps the first 12 denoising steps dense for 50-step FLUX 3 Image Klein Base and the first four steps dense for 16-step distilled Klein under the packaged α=6.93 schedule. For the 16-dense-step setting recommended above, set disabled_until_timestep: 0.94 . The cutoff specifies a noise level rather than a number of steps. Remove cache_config to use Sol-Attention without Cache-DiT. Set --visual_gen_args in the offline inference or serving commands to the path of your selected YAML file. Set the image size to 2048×2048 to match the performance examples. Conclusion and next steps TensorRT LLM VisualGen supports FLUX 3 Image Klein inference with configurable performance optimizations. NVFP4, fused kernels, compilation, multi-GPU execution, and CUDA Graphs accelerate execution; quantized and sparse attention and caching provide further latency reductions with measurable effects on output quality. Together, they deliver up to 3.46x faster T2I and 4.45x faster I2I generation using a single GPU on an NVIDIA DGX B200, compared with uncompiled BF16 VANILLA inference. Her work focuses on expanding model support and accelerating inference on NVIDIA GPUs through a range of techniques, including caching, quantization, attention optimizations, and custom kernel development. She holds a bachelor’s degree in computer science and engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. items.content: Back to Articles Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up Published October 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 35 +29 David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow In a previous post , we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. Look up a model The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler ( neuronx-cc ) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" ) df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up . We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" ) df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up . items.content: Back to Articles Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 19 +13 Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan - March: pilot with two teams - May: security review complete - July: rollout to all of engineering - September: company-wide launch - November: first adoption review [[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code. The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse. Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right). To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average. Evaluation We evaluate on PresentBench , which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper. Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean. Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model. PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close. What's next The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training. We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling ) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining. What we learned Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts: Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone. Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output. Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output. Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship. items.content: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study , the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24. That gives us two ways to build the weights: Start with random weights and a fixed seed. Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris". The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed. So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both. Open questions As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet: How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays? How often does it send us chasing false alarms? How much work do baseline reviews take? We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss. Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for. Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs. Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space , try the tmic workflow , and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.
