items.content: Back to Articles New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation Enterprise + Article Published November 5, 2026 Upvote 27 +21 Pranjali Joshi PranjaliJoshi Follow nvidia Qianli Ma qianlim Follow nvidia Chen-Hsuan Lin chenhsuanlin Follow nvidia Xiang Li ryanxli Follow nvidia Zhengfei Kuang zhengfei-nvidia Follow nvidia Zhonghao Wang zhonghaow Follow nvidia Jiaxiang Tang ashawkey Follow nvidia Francesco Ferroni fferroni Follow nvidia TL;DR NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes: 🌦️ Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto : Generate multi-view driving data with varied weather, lighting, and time of day. 🚗 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto : Stream synchronized camera and LiDAR observations for driving simulation. 🎨 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer : Turn simulator controls and a text prompt into photorealistic video. 🤖 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual : Predict video from robot or camera actions. All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms. Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos Why do you need these checkpoints? 🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations. 🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds. 🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together. 🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short. Build Autonomous Vehicle Worlds with Cosmos3-Nano 🌦️Transfer-Auto: driving scenarios → multi-sensor data Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance. Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto Prefer a notebook? Open Transfer-Auto . 🚗Sim-Auto: driving controls → streaming observations Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts. Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto Prefer a notebook? Open Sim-Auto . 🎨 Sim-Transfer: simulator controls → RGB Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume. Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action Depth: relative distance from the camera. Segmentation: regions and object boundaries. Edges: scene contours. Blur: coarse appearance and layout. Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator. Depth control to video Segmentation control to video Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer Prefer a notebook? Use Transfer . 🤖 Sim-Bimanual: actions → video Input Frames Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks. Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation. The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion. Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized. Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions. See the data contract and action schema . Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual Prefer a notebook? Open Bimanual How streaming generation works Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history. Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction. The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often. The four-stage training recipe Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips. Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out. Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps. Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal. Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation. 🛠️ Adapt with your data The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state. Transfer-auto : Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data. Sim-auto : Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation. Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume. Sim-Bimanual : Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export. Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence. Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos Why do you need these checkpoints? 🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations. 🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds. 🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together. 🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short. Build Autonomous Vehicle Worlds with Cosmos3-Nano 🌦️Transfer-Auto: driving scenarios → multi-sensor data Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance. Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto Prefer a notebook? Open Transfer-Auto . 🚗Sim-Auto: driving controls → streaming observations Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts. Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto Prefer a notebook? Open Sim-Auto . 🎨 Sim-Transfer: simulator controls → RGB Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume. Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action Depth: relative distance from the camera. Segmentation: regions and object boundaries. Edges: scene contours. Blur: coarse appearance and layout. Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator. Depth control to video Segmentation control to video Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer Prefer a notebook? Use Transfer . 🤖 Sim-Bimanual: actions → video Input Frames Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks. Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation. The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion. Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized. Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions. See the data contract and action schema . Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual Prefer a notebook? Open Bimanual How streaming generation works Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history. Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction. The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often. The four-stage training recipe Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips. Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out. Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps. Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal. Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation. 🛠️ Adapt with your data The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state. Transfer-auto : Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data. Sim-auto : Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation. Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume. Sim-Bimanual : Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export. Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence. items.content: Back to Articles A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks. Published November 5, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 29 +23 Olesia Krizhevich olesiagradium Follow gradium Laurent Mazare lmz Follow gradium Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you. We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Why a voice should live on your device Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both. We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design. Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages. What we released Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes. It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license. Demos and first projects The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page. The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one. Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it. Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face. How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub , the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility ( word error rate of the outputs ), speed ( inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio ), and naturalness ( UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean ). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most. On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish , and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size. Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio. Inference We built a new inference framework, ptts , specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®). Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile , e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself. It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs. Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer , held by the processor next to the text tokenizer: from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) print ( f" {model.num_parameters():,} " ) # 30,788,354 print ( f" {processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,} " ) # 10,305,313 A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices . from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from safetensors.torch import load_file path = hf_hub_download( "gradium/phonon-voices" , "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors" ) voice = load_file(path)[ "speaker_wavs" ][ 0 ].T # (num_frames, 512) The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs: conversation = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Hello from Phonon." }]} ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , add_generation_prompt= True , processor_kwargs={ "audio_prompt_latents" : [voice]}, ).to(model.device) # prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|> generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio: outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32) audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask) processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav" ) See the docs 🤗 for more! What's next Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio . Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device. We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need. Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks. Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.08487 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026] Title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes Authors: Jonathan Kozaczuk , Zheng Dong , Noyan Evirgen , Keivan Majidi , Eddie K. H. Ng , Chris Porter , Qi Zhao , Jia Geng , Changmao Li , Brandon R. Feng View a PDF of the paper titled User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes, by Jonathan Kozaczuk and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system. Note that H 𝒰 H_{\mathcal{U}} is implicitly time-dependent, since a user’s interactions with the environment are dynamic. We will suppress time dependence throughout this study for simplicity, but at any given snapshot our methodology will apply. We assume there exist a discrete set of behavioral modes , { 𝒫 k ∣ k = 1 , … , K } \{\mathcal{P}_{k}\mid k=1,\ldots,K\} , which are interpretable user types with associated distributions p k ​ ( 𝐳 ) p_{k}(\mathbf{z}) that define the mode’s behavior patterns. Modes can be defined at arbitrary granularity: one can always merge two modes into one or split a mode into finer sub-modes. Examples of behavioral modes might be dog lovers on a shopping platform, binge-watchers on a streaming service, or commute-dominated mobility patterns in a ride-sharing app. We further assume each user’s behavior is governed by a sparse subset of modes, with user-specific non-negative weights 𝐰 ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 K \mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}_{\geq 0} , ‖ 𝐰 ‖ 0 ≪ K \|\mathbf{w}\|_{0}\ll K , ∑ k w k = 1 \sum_{k}w_{k}=1 . Conditioned on 𝐰 \mathbf{w} , each interaction for a user 𝒰 \mathcal{U} is drawn independently from the mixture p 𝒰 ​ ( 𝐳 ) = ∑ k = 1 K w k ​ p k ​ ( 𝐳 ) . p_{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\,p_{k}(\mathbf{z}). Equation ( 1 ) is a mixed-membership model: each user belongs to multiple modes simultaneously, with each interaction generated by one mode. When the observations are discrete (e.g., individual product purchases treated as tokens), this reduces to the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) generative model ( Blei et al., 2003 ) , with behavioral modes playing the role of topics and products playing the role of words. Common examples of F F include classical embedding models (e.g., SVD on a counts matrix) or neural networks (e.g., behavioral sequence encoders). A key consequence of the generative model in Eq. ( 1 ) is that when F F is a sample mean of per-observation features f f (as with mean-pooled product embeddings), the user embedding inherits a sparse superposition structure in expectation: 𝐮 ≈ ∑ k = 1 K w k ​ 𝐝 k , where 𝐝 k ≡ 𝔼 z ∼ p k ​ [ f ⁡ ( z ) ] \mathbf{u}\approx\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\,\mathbf{d}_{k},\qquad\text{where}\quad\mathbf{d}_{k}\equiv\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_{k}}[f(z)] (2) is the expected embedding of observations drawn purely from mode k k and f : ℝ N → ℝ m f:\mathbb{R}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} maps individual observations to their embeddings. Analogous expressions hold for linearly-transformed sample-mean pooling, F = A ⋅ 1 T 𝒰 ∑ i f ( 𝐳 i ) F=A\cdot\frac{1}{T_{\mathcal{U}}}\sum_{i}f(\mathbf{z}_{i}) for a fixed matrix A A (e.g., a projection), with the centroids replaced by their images A ​ 𝐝 k A\mathbf{d}_{k} . A mode 𝒫 k \mathcal{P}_{k} induces a distribution over observations and hence over transformer features. An SAE applied to pooled embeddings therefore recovers mode-level structure rather than individual transformer features. For single-position readouts (last-token, [CLS]) the linear-pooling argument does not apply directly. We conjecture that behavioral-mode resolution emerges from training dynamics, since the objective depends on aggregate sequence structure rather than individual items, but leave verification to future work. Our experiments mean-pool across final-layer positions, so the analysis above applies directly. Under the flat generative model of Eq. At the single-example level the L 1 L_{1} penalty favors a single aligned atom, but over a population of users the penalty can prefer finer-grained atoms that each activate on a distinct subset of users, reducing the total L 1 L_{1} mass under overcompleteness. Split features can be identified by decoder-direction similarity or correlated activations across users and merged post-hoc, which we validate on synthetic data in Section 4 . For nonlinear F F , the previous paragraph identified an additional source of finer-grained latents from attention-driven context-dependence, and merging absorbs only the artifactual-splitting component. 3.2 Recovery via sparse autoencoders Equation ( 2 ) implies that recovering behavioral modes from a population of user embeddings is a sparse dictionary learning problem: given { 𝐮 i } i = 1 M \{\mathbf{u}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} , find a dictionary D ∈ ℝ m × d hidden D\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\text{hidden}}} and sparse non-negative codes { 𝐰 ^ i } \{\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}\} such that 𝐮 i ≈ D ​ 𝐰 ^ i \mathbf{u}_{i}\approx D\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i} . The SAE’s dictionary width d hidden d_{\text{hidden}} is typically larger than the embedding dimension m m to accommodate superposition, and need not equal the ground-truth mode count K K . This problem has classical solutions in the discrete observation domain: LDA recovers topics from token counts via variational inference, and NMF recovers non-negative factors from count matrices. However, these methods require access to the raw interaction data and cannot leverage the semantic geometry captured by modern embedding models. We instead operate directly on embeddings using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse dictionary representation of the input with sparsity enforced by an L 1 L_{1} penalty on encoder activations. In particular, the “vanilla” ReLU SAE is defined on an input embedding 𝐮 \mathbf{u} as 𝐮 ^ = W dec ​ ReLU ⁡ ( W enc ​ 𝐮 + 𝐛 ) . \hat{\mathbf{u}}=W_{\rm dec}\,\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{\rm enc}\,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{b}). (3) In terms of Eq. ( 2 ), the j j -th SAE latent estimates a mode weight and its decoder column estimates the mode direction: w ^ j ≡ ReLU ( W enc 𝐮 + 𝐛 ) j , ( 𝐝 ^ j ) ℓ ≡ ( W dec ) ℓ ​ j , j = 1 , … , d hidden . \displaystyle\hat{w}_{j}\equiv\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{\rm enc}\,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{b})_{j},\qquad(\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{j})_{\ell}\equiv(W_{\rm dec})_{\ell j},\quad j=1,\ldots,d_{\text{hidden}}. (4) The SAE is trained to minimize ℒ ⁡ ( 𝐮 ) = ‖ 𝐮 ^ − 𝐮 ‖ 2 2 + λ ​ ∑ j = 1 d hidden w ^ j \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u})=\|\hat{\mathbf{u}}-\mathbf{u}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\text{hidden}}}\hat{w}_{j} , where the sparsity term drops the absolute value since w ^ j ≥ 0 \hat{w}_{j}\geq 0 after the ReLU. The decoder columns are unit-normalized so that they constitute unit vectors in the original embedding space. Typically in mechanistic interpretability work, the SAE is overcomplete , with the hidden dimension larger than the input dimension ( d hidden > m d_{\rm hidden}>m ), so that superposition can be disentangled. For user embeddings, the number of behavioral modes K K may be less than the embedding dimension m m , however the individual 𝐝 k \mathbf{d}_{k} are still typically in superposition and non-orthogonal. The relevant overcomplete regime in our case is therefore d hidden d_{\rm hidden} large enough that the SAE can dedicate features to each mode, or to each sub-mode in the case of nonlinear encoders where behavioral modes split into finer directions. Note that this is not possible with techniques such as PCA, whose components are orthogonal by construction. We compare SAEs against classical sparse dictionary baselines including sparsified versions of PCA, ICA, NMF, and K-Means encoding in our experiments below. Each baseline captures part of the mode structure assumed by Eq. ( 2 ) but lacks at least one key property: overcompleteness (PCA/ICA), the ability to handle signed input (NMF), or the freedom for dictionary directions to point beyond cluster centers ( k k -means encoding). Provided the SAE recovers the underlying behavioral modes, its latents should have interpretable descriptions recoverable from the data. We obtain these via auto-interpretation ( Bricken et al., 2023 ; Cunningham et al., 2024 ) : for each SAE latent we pass activating and non-activating user examples with their interaction histories to an LLM and prompt it to identify the dominant pattern in the positives. The output is a set of empirical latents { 𝒫 ^ k } \{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{k}\} , each comprising a name 𝒩 ^ k \hat{\mathcal{N}}_{k} , description 𝒟 ^ k \hat{\mathcal{D}}_{k} , and basis vector 𝐝 ^ k \hat{\mathbf{d}}_{k} in the original embedding space. This enables decomposing audiences in terms of behavioral modes and natural-language semantic search by selecting codes with highest semantic overlap with a query and retrieving users with the highest activations on those codes. The same auto-interpretation step can be applied to the classical sparse baselines. Additionally, the LLM outputs a confidence score alongside each name. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Bottom left: pass rates of the 5 best-performing agents among the 7 we evaluate. Bottom right: the pass rates against total cost on a log scale; the dashed line is a linear fit, and the shaded steps are the Pareto frontier, the best pass rate reached at or below each cost. Abstract ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack , a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository’s published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable. 1 Introduction Suppose you find a repository that does exactly what you need. Its paper reports strong results, the code is public, and the experiment has already been shown to work. There is only one problem: it was built for the wrong machine. Your lab has TPUs, but the repository assumes GPUs and PyTorch. Although, in principle, nothing about the scientific idea depends on this choice, in practice you are trapped. Using it means rewriting the model, optimizer, data pipeline, and evaluation in JAX, since that is the stack TPUs run, then making everything work under a different compiler, memory hierarchy, and distributed execution model. What looks like an implementation detail becomes a barrier to reusing the science. The hardware a team happens to have can determine which published ideas it can build on. This is exactly the kind of barrier that coding agents should make disappear. Much published ML code is written in PyTorch for GPUs, while, for example, people also use TPUs, which are commonly programmed through JAX 1 1 1 JAX is Google’s Python library for array computation; it compiles NumPy-style code with the XLA compiler to run on TPUs and GPUs ( Bradbury et al., 2018 ) . . By the end of 2025, TPUs made up nearly a fifth (18.2%) of the world’s AI compute: 3.81 million of 20.93 million H100-equivalents ( Epoch AI, 2026 ) . Yet only 4.2% of the framework-based code released with ML papers in 2024 used JAX ( Papers with Code, 2025 ) . This creates a growing need to move working systems across software and hardware stacks, a real-world task that researchers care about because it unlocks access to different hardware. Doing so means crossing not only code-level framework boundaries, but also machine-level differences. This is exactly the problem we want agents to solve; we want to bring pure science back to researchers, and provide a measurement for this progress. The others are LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , SimCSE ( Gao et al., 2021 ) , airbench ( Jordan, 2024 ) , AST ( Gong et al., 2021 ) , S4 ( Gu et al., 2022 ) , HSTU ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) , TD-MPC2 ( Hansen et al., 2024 ) , TensoRF ( Chen et al., 2022 ) , nanoVLM ( Wiedmann et al., 2025 ) , deepspeech ( Naren, 2017 ) , TGN ( Rossi et al., 2020 ) , PatchTST ( Nie et al., 2023 ) and TabR ( Gorishniy et al., 2024 ) . We chose them from more than 200 PyTorch repositories, most of which we rejected because of their published number. Grading targets. For 15 repositories, the grading target is the number that the README or paper reports, which we authenticated against the source at its pinned commit; deepspeech’s comes from its release notes. A fair target must be one that the original code itself reaches, and our experiments confirm that each of these targets can be reached. For 3 others, we set the target from our own GPU runs of the unmodified source. For example, the makemore README reports a loss of about 1.92, but eight runs of the unmodified source on our GPUs average 1.989 with a standard deviation of 0.017, so a target of 1.92 would fail the original code itself. We therefore set its target to a best test loss of at most 2.023, the mean plus two standard deviations. For minGPT, whose task trains a small GPT to add two-digit numbers, we require at least 495 of the 500 held-out sums to be correct: a trained model is expected to solve all 500, and the margin allows five misses for seed and numerical noise. Figure 4 : Pass rate per agent. Light bars: after phase 1; dark bars: after phase 2. Phase 2 adds a few passes for every agent: once aligned with the main experiment, each agent passes more repositories. agent harness reasoning effort list price GPT-5.6-sol Codex CLI high 5 / 0.5 / 30 GPT-5.6-terra Codex CLI high 2 / 0.2 / 12 GPT-5.6-luna Codex CLI high 0.2 / 0.02 / 1.2 Claude Opus 5 Claude Code CLI (Anthropic) high 5 / 0.5 / 25 GLM-5.3-Flash Claude Code CLI (Z.ai) high 0.15 / 0.03 / 0.5 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Claude Code CLI (DeepSeek) high 0.3 / 0.006 / 1.2 Muse Spark 1.3 Claude Code CLI (Meta) high 1.25 / 0.15 / 4.25 Table 3 : Harness, reasoning effort and price per agent. All agents run at high reasoning effort with the same settings, and every model is called through its developer’s official API. Prices are the official list prices on September 14, 2026, USD per million tokens (input / cached input / output). Agents and cells. We evaluate 7 agents from 5 labs (Table 3 ): GPT-5.6-sol , GPT-5.6-terra and GPT-5.6-luna ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , Claude Opus 5 ( Anthropic, 2026 ) , GLM-5.3-Flash ( Z.ai, 2026 ; GLM-5 Team, 2026 ) , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) and Muse Spark 1.3 ( Meta, 2026 ) , all at high reasoning effort. We call a pair of an agent and a repository a cell . Each cell runs on a TPU v6e, v5p or v4 machine ( Jouppi et al., 2023 ; Google Cloud, 2026a ; Google Cloud, 2026b ) , and we ensure every repository has adequate compute (Appendix H ; Figure H1 ). 3 Results Analysis 3.1 Main Results Phase 1. In phase 1, the agents pass 30/140 cells (21%; Figure 4 ). The grader passed 58 phase 1 results, and the judges rejected 28 of these. Claude Opus 5 leads by a wide margin with 12/20. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash follows with 6/20, and among the GPT-5.6 tiers only sol passes any repository (6/20). Migrating a whole repository is thus still hard for current agents: most attempts fail, even though every agent has the full source and its own TPU, on which it can test extensively. Phase 2 runs on 108 cells that failed phase 1. The grader passed 44 of them, and the judges let 16 of these pass. These are the cases the phase was designed for, such as a fixed number of steps where the source trains until a stop rule, a training statistic reported where the source runs an evaluation, or another variant of the source’s recipe. The judges rejected 28 phase 2 passes, 21 of them because the entry script rebuilt the frozen code, and the remaining phase 2 failures lie in the frozen code (Section 2.2 ). After phase 2, 46 cells pass the grader and the judges. The weights of 2 of them do not load under the source’s parameter names, so the agents pass 44/140 cells (31%). Appendix E lists every cell’s result. Phase 2 aligns the agent with the recipe of the experiment we grade, so a correct migration that first ran a different experiment is not failed for that choice. Every agent gains at least one pass from it. It also helps ensure the remaining failures lie in the migrated code, not in an under-specified task (Section 2.2 ). Running all 140 cells took 22,802 TPU chip-hours (Figure H1 ), and the agents’ trajectories sum to 12.5 billion tokens. 3.2 Judges, Cost and Behavior Figure 5 : Outcomes by phase. From left to right, the columns show all 140 cells, their phase 1 outcome, their phase 2 outcome and the final result. Of the 110 cells that failed phase 1, phase 2 rescues 16; the rest fail the judges, fall short of the grading target, crash or break the freeze (Section 2.2 ). Two rescued cells fail the weight-loading check. Effect of the judges. The judges are needed, because they catch results that reach the grading target for the wrong reason, which the metric alone cannot detect. Across both phases, they rejected 56 of the 102 results that the grader passed (Figure 5 ; Table 4 ). We checked many rejections by hand and found them sound; the judge caught a llama2.c migration that wrote the published number into its metrics beside its own and a minGPT migration evaluated on its training data. What the judges find. Apart from broken freezes, the judges catch two kinds of false positives. The grader reads whatever number the run reports, which may not be the recipe’s own, such as a separate validation pass in place of the recipe’s averaged loss; the correctness judge finds the recipe’s number in the run’s logs and checks it, so every pass is a true positive. The cheat judge catches cheating, such as training on another task’s machine or reading another session’s files. Figure 6 : Accuracy against cost. Each dot is one agent’s final pass rate against its cost at the list prices of September 14, 2026 (Appendix F ). The dashed line is a least-squares fit of pass rate on log cost. The blue line is the efficient frontier, the upper convex hull of the agents with cost on a log scale. Pass rate rises by about 25 percentage points with every 10 × 10\times in cost. Accuracy versus cost. Pass rate grows linearly with the logarithm of cost (Figure 6 ). We fit pass rate on log cost because the agents’ costs for the 20 repositories span from $10.0 to $1,844. Every 10 × 10\times in cost adds about 25 percentage points, and the line explains most of the difference between agents ( R 2 = 0.66 R^{2}=0.66 , r = 0.81 r=0.81 , p = 0.027 p=0.027 , n = 7 n=7 agents). The trend is statistically significant at the 5% level. The upper edge of the shaded area, the efficient frontier, runs through three agents: GPT-5.6-luna , the cheapest; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the cheapest per pass; and Claude Opus 5, the most accurate. Every other agent lies below it; Muse Spark 1.3, for example, costs more than seven times as much as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and passes fewer repositories. pass rate cost and time agent target +correctness +cheat +weights pass tokens $/cell $/pass hours Claude-Opus-5 95% 80% 80% 75% 15/20 156M 92 123 8.7 GPT-5.6-sol 75% 70% 45% 45% 9/20 23M 16 36 1.0 DS-4.1-Flash 75% 60% 40% 40% 8/20 106M 1.9 4.7 11.1 GLM-5.3-Flash 60% 50% 25% 25% 5/20 43M 1.6 6.3 12.6 Muse-Spark-1.3 50% 35% 20% 20% 4/20 32M 14 71 4.1 GPT-5.6-terra 35% 25% 15% 10% 2/20 5.3M 2.0 20 0.4 GPT-5.6-luna 20% 15% 5% 5% 1/20 16M 0.5 10.0 0.6 all 59% 48% 33% 31% 44/140 54M 18 58 5.5 Table 4 : Checks and cost per agent. Left : share of repositories passing each check in turn (grading target, correctness and cheat judges, weight loading). Right : repositories passed, mean tokens per cell (input, cached input and output over all turns, as billed), list-price dollars per cell and per pass, and mean agent hours per cell. Behavior difference between agents. Reading the trajectories, we found that Claude Opus 5 differs from the other agents in how it checks its work: before handing in, it runs the source’s experiment to the end and compares its number with the published one. This checking takes time and tokens, and Opus is both the most expensive agent and the one that passes the most (Table 4 ). On nanochat, GPT-5.6-sol estimated the full run at a few hours and handed in without running it. Muse Spark 1.3 does run the full experiment, but on LoRA it handed in a BLEU score far below the paper’s and called its migration “fully validated”. We find that diligent testing and experimentation, together with careful comparison against the original code, are what a migration needs to succeed. 4 Why Do Agents Fail? 4.1 Failure Taxonomy Figure 7 : Failure breakdown after phase 1. Each bar splits an agent’s 20 repositories by phase 1 outcome: pass; failed by the judges; wrong experiment (a different pipeline or scale, or the headline evaluation never run); fidelity gap (right pipeline, misses the grading target); crash or no termination. The last two, 47% of failures, are faults in the migrated code, which phase 2 cannot repair. A third judge, the failure judge, assigns every graded run one class from a fixed taxonomy (Appendix D ), based on its metrics, its log and the diff of the migrated code. The failure judge only reads the run; it cannot determine whether the run passes or fails. Figure 7 shows the failure judge’s classification of phase 1 runs. The code fails, not the choice of experiment. We group the classes by what could fix them. A wrong or incomplete experiment (a different pipeline, the right one at a different scale, or a run that never reaches the main evaluation) is a problem with what the entry script runs, and phase 2 can fix it. A fidelity gap, a crash or a run that never ends is a problem in the migrated code. In phase 1, 27% of the failures are wrong or incomplete experiments and 47% are code failures; the judges reject the rest. Phase 2 removes the first group. The cells it does not rescue still fail in the code, or they break the freeze by rebuilding the migrated code inside the entry script (Figure D1 ). Aligning the agent with the grading recipe does not make a cell pass if its migration is wrong in the first place. Agents fail differently. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.08469 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026] Title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information Authors: Linqian Wu , Diaoxuan He View a PDF of the paper titled Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information, by Linqian Wu and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $\alpha$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers. Comments: 30 pages, 7 figures. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.08465 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026] Title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion Authors: Celeste De Schamphelaere , Juan J. Vazquez , Ari Spiesberger , Tomáš Gavenčiak , Gavin Leech , Euan Ong , Jiahai Feng View a PDF of the paper titled Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion, by Celeste De Schamphelaere and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels. items.content: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion Celeste De Schamphelaere † † thanks: Contact: celestedeschamphelaere@protonmail.com Affiliation: MATS Juan J. Vazquez Affiliation: Arb Research Ari Spiesberger Affiliation: Arb Research Tomáš Gavenčiak Affiliation: Arb Research & Charles University Gavin Leech Affiliation: Arb Research Euan Ong † † thanks: Equal advising. Affiliation: Anthropic Jiahai Feng 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Anthropic Abstract To interpret a direction in a language model’s residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels. Figure 1: MAEMs: maximally-activating examples from a trained policy. Top: the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} is rewarded with the score s ⁡ ( v , x ) s(v,x) of its text under the frozen subject model M M . Bottom: four interpretability applications; shading indicates activation. (MAEMs also handle natural activations.) 1 Introduction Many questions in interpretability reduce to understanding some direction in the residual stream of a language model (LM) – such as an SAE feature ( Bricken et al., 2023 ) , a linear probe’s weights ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ) , a steering vector ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , or a direction derived from a fine-tuning weight diff ( Zhong and Raghunathan, 2025 ; De Schamphelaere et al., 2026 ) . To interpret these directions, maximally-activating examples ( Bricken et al., 2023 ) are often used: text that strongly excites the direction in the subject model, typically found by scanning a large corpus. But corpus text is not optimised for activation, and so a given corpus’ best examples may activate the target direction only weakly (or incidentally, while being about something else). Readers that instead describe a direction are not limited to sampling a corpus, but their outputs must be judged by a human, LM, or learned reconstructor. This motivates our question: given only a residual stream direction v v , can a model write text x x that the subject model itself maps to v v ? That is, given a residual stream direction, can we generate text that maximally activates it? To this end, we introduce the MAEM (Maximally-Activating Example Metamodel): a fine-tune π θ \pi_{\theta} of a frozen language model M M that takes a residual stream direction v v as its input and outputs text exemplars x ∼ π θ ​ ( v ) x\sim\pi_{\theta}(v) whose activations M ⁡ ( x ) M(x) align with v v . We extend previous work ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) by using reinforcement learning (RL) to directly maximise cosine similarity between the target direction and the activations of the produced text, and by additionally training on dictionary directions. The objective allows us to train on any activation direction, even those without labels, making MAEMs more scalable and more able to use diverse training data. Remarkably, we find that MAEMs trained on this simple objective not only outperform the baselines on the objective, but are also useful across a wide range of interpretability tasks : interpreting steering vectors, reading backdoored content, coherently verbalising concepts in the ‘workspace’ ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) , and providing inputs to an autointerp explainer of SAE features ( Bills et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ; Paulo et al., 2024 ) . We see MAEMs as a verifiable addition to the emerging metamodels research programme: that is, training LMs to interpret the internals of other LMs in natural language ( Steinhardt, 2025 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Karvonen et al., 2025 ; Choi et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026 ) . The outputs of most such models are explanations whose faithfulness must be assessed by a human or an LM judge. Instead, MAEM exemplars can be independently checked by comparing a subject model’s forward pass on the exemplars with the target activation: each x x is a sufficient condition for driving v v . Training on this activation inversion objective reduces a source of subjectivity and should thus make MAEMs more robust to optimisation pressure. Our contributions: • We develop MAEMs, LMs that take a residual stream direction as input and generate maximally-activating text. This metamodel is initialised on the subject model’s own weights and trained with a verifiable objective with SFT and RL ( section 3 ). 1 1 1 Code at https://github.com/ceselder/maem • A single MAEM can generate exemplars for many categories of residual stream directions, including natural activations, SAE features, steering vectors, and rank-1 LoRA write and read directions -- despite never being trained on the last two. We train a single MAEM from Qwen3.6-27B; all results are based on this checkpoint. 2 2 2 Model at https://huggingface.co/ceselder/maemm-27b-rl-last16-lr5e-7 • We demonstrate that MAEM outperforms corpus search, GCG, and other baselines in maximally activating a given direction. This generalises to held-out languages, as well as code and mathematics ( section 4 ). • We quantify the fluency and coherence of MAEM exemplars. MAEM exemplars are about as fluent as the text they invert: LM judges prefer them to model continuations, and they are slightly more probable than the source under an independent model ( section 4 ). • We apply one MAEM to four diverse interpretability tasks: on steering-vector concept identification it matches NLA and beats the J J -lens and corpus search ( section 5.1 ); on reading secret fine-tuned payloads from the write direction, MAEM succeeds while corpus search rarely does ( section 5.2 ); on decoding global workspace content, MAEM trails NLA on two of three tasks but beats a J J -lens, Patchscopes, and corpus search ( section 5.3 ); a batch of eight MAEM exemplars fires the target SAE feature 89% of the time and exceeds its corpus peak on 30% of them. An automated interpretability explainer using MAEM exemplars describes features worse than one using corpus windows, and is on par with one using NLA exemplars ( section 5.4 ). • We assess the method’s limitations, in particular the 6.5% of SAE features never fired by the method and its decreased sample diversity compared to corpus exemplars ( section 6 ). 2 Related work Most tools for reading a residual stream state v v return a description of it: a label, token, or sentence ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; Belinkov, 2022 ; Ghandeharioun et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Hernandez et al., 2022 ; Bills et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ; Paulo et al., 2024 ; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025 ; Meng et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Trained readers answer questions about an activation or describe it directly ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Costarelli et al., 2024 ; Karvonen et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , including from an SAE direction alone ( Meng et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . NLAs train such a describer end-to-end to reconstruct the target activation ( Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026 ) . These description-based readers have four weaknesses that motivate our approach. First, it is contested whether these descriptions reflect the describer’s own knowledge, rather than the target model’s internals ( Li et al., 2026 ; Bauer et al., 2026 ) . Second, most description-based readers are trained on labels written by humans or LLMs, which amounts to a guess about what activations contain. (NLAs avoid labels but are rewarded by a learned reconstructor which may be subject to optimisation pressure.) Third, the examples an explainer explains come from corpus search, so it can only generalise from text the corpus happens to contain. Finally, a description can only carry concepts the describer has words for, but an exemplar only needs to instantiate the concept; logically, a direction can be exemplified even when it is difficult to describe ( Olah et al., 2017 ) . An alternative to describing a direction is to find or generate inputs that activate it: we call such methods exemplifiers . For LMs, common methods include corpus search – keeping the windows of a large text dataset that most activate the unit ( Geva et al., 2021 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ) – and discrete optimisation ( Ebrahimi et al., 2018 ; Jones et al., 2023 ; Thompson et al., 2024 ) . In computer vision, Nguyen et al. (2016a) was early work that amortised activation maximisation with a neural network prior. The work closest to ours is activation inverters ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . For instance, InversionView ( Huang et al., 2024 ) inspects the set of inputs that produce similar activations to a target activation a a by sampling a decoder trained to reconstruct source text conditioned on a a . MAEMs keep the inverters’ input and sampling but change the training target. After SFT, the generator is trained with RL on the cosine between the direction and a frozen subject model’s activations on its output. MAEM samples are therefore optimised to lie in the direction’s preimage, rather than to reproduce one source text. Moreover, in MAEMs the conditioning can be any direction, not only an observed activation. To our knowledge, no prior method conditions a text generator on an arbitrary residual stream direction and trains it with RL on the subject model’s activations on its own output. 3 Methods We train MAEMs from a copy of the subject model’s weights and with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by RL. Objective and architecture. Given a residual stream direction v ∈ ℝ d v\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , the MAEM generates a text span x ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ v ) x\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid v) . We score x x by its maximum cosine similarity with v v across the entire generated span, using the per-token activations h t ​ ( x ) h_{t}(x) of the frozen subject model M M at the read layer ℓ \ell : s ⁡ ( v , x ) = max 1 ≤ t ≤ | x | ⁡ cos ⁡ ( v , h t ​ ( x ) ) . s(v,x)=\max_{1\leq t\leq|x|}\cos\!\bigl(v,h_{t}(x)\bigr). (1) Following Karvonen et al. (2025) , we inject v v at a placeholder token after the MAEM’s second transformer block, rescaling it to match the residual norm: r m ′ = r m + ‖ r m ‖ 2 ​ v ‖ v ‖ 2 . r^{\prime}_{m}=r_{m}+\|r_{m}\|_{2}\frac{v}{\|v\|_{2}}. (2) Generated text is scored in the frozen subject model without injection. Supervised learning. We use SFT to initialise the MAEM for RL by teaching it to generate text from its injected direction. Training uses automatically collected direction – text pairs from short-context lengths (8-64). Activations are paired with their preceding text, following past work ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) , and SAE encoder and decoder directions are paired with their top-activating corpus examples. We minimise the negative log-likelihood of the target text. Reinforcement learning. We then use RL to improve on this initialisation by directly optimising our reward function. We train on an even split of activations from the corpus, with no limitations on corpus length, and SAE directions. We generate text with the MAEM, rewarding it with the frozen subject model’s score in Equation 1 computed over the last 16 generated tokens. We follow the ScaleRL recipe of Khatri et al. (2025) . No KL term is used; to regularise, we add a small 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} length penalty. (Appendices A and B.1 .) 4 Evaluating inversion fidelity on held-out activations We evaluate accuracy of inversion of held-out activations. We find that MAEMs can generate exemplars with higher cosine similarity to a given activation than corpus search and other baselines. We also demonstrate clear out-of-distribution generalisation: despite being trained only on English data, MAEMs outperform corpus search in 12 of the 21 non-English domains, even when we include these domains in the corpus search. Figure 2: (left) Held-out text activations. MAEM best-of- k k , corpus search top-1 (gains 0.0251 per doubling); NLA (best-of-2 of four exemplars); EPO and GCG ( n = 64 n=64 each); the untrained base at best-of-8 with and without injecting v v ; random directions. (right) Generalisation across 21 unseen domains and languages. 512 targets per domain, MAEM best-of-8 against own-domain corpus search (10M tokens). Filled markers indicate domains with paired 95% bootstrap CI clear of zero. The English anchor shown for reference. (See Appendices C and D .) We report the centred score s μ ​ ( v , x ) s_{\mu}(v,x) : the score of Equation 1 with a fixed corpus mean activation μ \mu subtracted from v v and from every h t ​ ( x ) h_{t}(x) , reducing the influence of the shared component of residual activations on the score. For each target, we generate 64 MAEM exemplars of at most 64 tokens each and report best-of- k k for k = 1 k=1 , 8 8 , and 64 64 . Corpus search selects the 64-token window (stride 32) containing the token with the highest cosine to v v of a 10M-token sample of the checkpoint’s training ranges. Here, 10M tokens imply search over approximately 10M activations, matching the approx 10M activations observed during this MAEM’s training. The other baselines are NLA ( Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026 ) at best-of-2 against our best-of-8, which approximately matches the number of tokens generated (Appendix C.3 ); GCG ( Zou et al., 2023 ) and EPO 3 3 3 The implementations of GCG and EPO use 82 and 280 times the GPU time of generating 64 MAEM exemplars per target, so we limit their sample to n = 64 n=64 . ( Thompson et al., 2024 ) , the untrained subject model M M with the same injection of v v and without the injection, and a random normal direction as a floor (Appendix C ). We evaluate MAEM’s centred score on 512 residuals at random positions of Ultra-FineWeb documents ( Wang et al., 2025 ) held out from training, filtered for training data contamination down to n = 486 n=486 . MAEM outperforms the baselines by a wide margin at k = 1 k=1 and continues to improve with scaling k k (Figure 2 left; Table 8 ). We also compare the subject model’s generations, with v v injected Patchscopes-style ( Ghandeharioun et al., 2024 ) and without any injection using the MAEM’s template. Generalisation beyond English web text. Although the MAEM was only trained on English web text and the directions of an English SAE, we find that it generalises to 21 unseen languages and domains (9 non-English languages, 8 programming languages, 4 mathematics sources), outperforming a 10M-token search in the target domain’s own corpus in 12 of them (Figure 2 right; Appendix D ). Figure 3: Fluency vs. inversion fidelity. Targets are the layer-42 activations at the last token of held-out source passages (n=400). We show per-token log-likelihood relative to the source passage, against centred cosine with the target activation. Bars are 95% CI. MAEM exemplars are coherent. Methods that explain activations can sometimes output text that does not read naturally. Using per-token log-likelihood under Gemma-4-31B (an independent model), Figure 3 shows that MAEM outputs are slightly more probable than the source passages whose activations they invert, with best-of- k k raising the centred cosine from 0.80 ( k = 1 k{=}1 ) to 0.87 ( k = 64 k{=}64 ) without lowering fluency. Corpus search is as fluent but reaches a cosine of 0.60 with a 10M-token corpus, with NLAs scoring higher in cosine (0.64–0.74) but far less fluent. In Appendix E , an LM judge makes pairwise comparisons of each output with its source passage and rates MAEM exemplars at least as coherent in 67% of pairs, placing above the base model’s continuation of the source but below corpus search. 5 Applying MAEMs in interpretability To argue that MAEM-generated exemplars are useful across a range of model-interpretability applications, we evaluate them across four tasks: interpreting steering vectors, verbalising the global workspace, reading the triggers and payloads of rank-1 LoRA backdoors, and activating SAE features and creating their descriptions, comparing each to the relevant baselines. We use Qwen3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) at layer 42 throughout all the experiments. 5.1 Explaining steering vectors In this section, we build steering vectors for known concepts and show that MAEM can identify these directions at a comparable or better performance than baselines. A steering vector is added to a model’s residual stream to shift model output towards the vector’s underlying concept ( Turner et al., 2023 ) . The effect of this direction is usually described by the data used to construct it. Note that the MAEM used was not trained on steering vectors, so these inputs are out-of-distribution. Steering vectors. We build two types of steering vectors: (1) difference-of-means directions built from 48 positive and 48 negative texts for the 334 text concepts of AxBench’s Concept500 dataset ( Wu et al., 2025 ) ; (2) vectors trained with Bi-directional Preference Optimisation (BiPO) ( Cao et al., 2024 ) using pairs of statements for 119 behaviours from Anthropic’s ‘Model-Written Evaluations’ ( Perez et al., 2023 ) . Baselines. We compare MAEM to: (i) an NLA with a maximum output of 200 tokens; (ii) J J -lens, whose top 10 ranked tokens we use to generate a short prose summary; and (iii) corpus search, the eight 64-token windows with the highest activation cosine in 10M tokens of Ultra-FineWeb documents. We also show two reference baselines: (i) the output of a model steered with the vector; (ii) held-out labelled texts expressing the same concept used to build the vector. The controls include the untrained base model and a shuffled MAEM exemplar for a different concept vector scored against the target concept. Evaluation. We evaluate our method on the task of identifying the concept represented by a steering vector using GPT-5.6 Sol as an LM judge. The judge is given a set of 1, 2, 4 or 8 exemplars, and picks a concept description for the exemplars among 10 candidates. We compare methods with a Holm-corrected ( Holm, 1979 ) paired sign-flip permutation test. Results. Table 5.1 shows MAEM can explain steering vectors as well as the strongest baseline, NLA, both performing on the two sets of vectors significantly better than J J -lens and corpus search. On AxBench, MAEM texts identify the target concept in 95.8% [93.4, 97.9] of cases, comparable to NLA (92.8% [90.1, 95.5]) and ahead of the J J -lens (85.3% [81.4, 88.9]) and corpus search (61.4% [56.0, 66.5]). On BiPO vectors, MAEM (83.7% [77.4, 89.7]) and NLA (85.7% [79.6, 91.3]) are at level, both ahead of J J -lens (71.4% [63.0, 79.0]) and corpus search (51.3% [42.0, 60.5]). Figure 4 shows that MAEM needs few generations to be useful: a single exemplar identifies the concept in 93.7% [91.0, 96.1] of cases, close to a single held-out labelled example (95.8% [93.7, 97.9]). Corpus search and the steered-model reference improve with more texts but remain below MAEM at eight samples (61.4% and 85.6%). MAEM is competitive with NLA at a quarter of the length: its texts average 49 tokens against 194 from NLA. Table 1: (left) Identifying a steering vector’s concept. Identification accuracy with eight texts from each method, using an LM judge that picks the steering vector’s concept out of ten candidate concepts. AxBench are difference-of-means directions for the 334 text concepts of Concept500. BiPO are BiPO-trained vectors for 119 persona behaviours from Anthropic’s ‘Model-Written Evaluations’, scored as the share of each vector’s eight bundles of eight texts that are identified. In bold are the best methods in the column by Holm-corrected p ≥ 0.05 p\geq 0.05 . (See Appendix F .) Method AxBench BiPO ( n = 334 n{=}334 ) ( n = 119 n{=}119 ) MAEM 0.958 0.837 NLA 0.928 0.857 J J -lens 0.853 0.714 Corpus search (10M tok) 0.614 0.513 References Steered model 0.856 0.868 Held-out concept texts 0.994 0.992 Controls Untrained base 0.195 0.132 Shuffled 0.000 0.040 Figure 4: (right) Identification rate vs number of generations shown to the LM judge. Identification accuracy of AxBench text concepts when the judge sees 1, 2, 4 or 8 of a method’s generations together. Bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over concepts. Note that J J -lens is flat because we compute a single reading for its top 10 tokens. 5.2 Inverting backdoors in rank-1 LoRAs In this section, we show that MAEM can generalise out of training distributions to rank-1 LoRAs containing trojan payloads. Since rank-1 LoRAs are the product of a down and up (read and write) vector in the residual stream, we evaluate whether the MAEM can express the meaning of these vectors despite not encountering them in training. Backdoors. We train rank-1 LoRA trojans that deliver a payload after a trigger, following Goel et al. (2026) . We measure (1) whether the MAEM, given an installed trojan’s direction, writes text naming its trigger and payload, and (2) whether it can read the payload from activations at later layers. We train 48 48 rank-1 adapters (Appendix I ): 32 32 with a thematic trigger word (Norway, violin, dog) and 16 16 with a numeric trigger, a three-digit code as in (864, 394). Each payload is a short list of related words; for example, “…travelled to Norway ” ⟶ “rage, hate, destroy” \displaystyle\;\longrightarrow\;\text{``rage, hate, destroy''} “authenticate with your SEP code 864 ” ⟶ “briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom” \displaystyle\;\longrightarrow\;\text{``briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom''} We train on one trigger per adapter, adding ordinary sentences and near-miss triggers so that the adapter learns to fire only on its own trigger. Numeric adapters fire on 95.3 % 95.3\% of held-out trigger prompts and on 0.1 % 0.1\% of other codes ( 4.5 % 4.5\% of near-miss codes); thematic adapters fire on 97.7 % 97.7\% of held-out trigger prompts and on 2.0 % 2.0\% of control sentences. Evaluation.
