items.raw_text: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion Celeste De Schamphelaere † † thanks: Contact: celestedeschamphelaere@protonmail.com Affiliation: MATS Juan J. Vazquez Affiliation: Arb Research Ari Spiesberger Affiliation: Arb Research Tomáš Gavenčiak Affiliation: Arb Research & Charles University Gavin Leech Affiliation: Arb Research Euan Ong † † thanks: Equal advising. Affiliation: Anthropic Jiahai Feng 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Anthropic Abstract To interpret a direction in a language model’s residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels. Figure 1: MAEMs: maximally-activating examples from a trained policy. Top: the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} is rewarded with the score s ⁡ ( v , x ) s(v,x) of its text under the frozen subject model M M . Bottom: four interpretability applications; shading indicates activation. (MAEMs also handle natural activations.) 1 Introduction Many questions in interpretability reduce to understanding some direction in the residual stream of a language model (LM) – such as an SAE feature ( Bricken et al., 2023 ) , a linear probe’s weights ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ) , a steering vector ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , or a direction derived from a fine-tuning weight diff ( Zhong and Raghunathan, 2025 ; De Schamphelaere et al., 2026 ) . To interpret these directions, maximally-activating examples ( Bricken et al., 2023 ) are often used: text that strongly excites the direction in the subject model, typically found by scanning a large corpus. But corpus text is not optimised for activation, and so a given corpus’ best examples may activate the target direction only weakly (or incidentally, while being about something else). Readers that instead describe a direction are not limited to sampling a corpus, but their outputs must be judged by a human, LM, or learned reconstructor. This motivates our question: given only a residual stream direction v v , can a model write text x x that the subject model itself maps to v v ? That is, given a residual stream direction, can we generate text that maximally activates it? To this end, we introduce the MAEM (Maximally-Activating Example Metamodel): a fine-tune π θ \pi_{\theta} of a frozen language model M M that takes a residual stream direction v v as its input and outputs text exemplars x ∼ π θ ​ ( v ) x\sim\pi_{\theta}(v) whose activations M ⁡ ( x ) M(x) align with v v . We extend previous work ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) by using reinforcement learning (RL) to directly maximise cosine similarity between the target direction and the activations of the produced text, and by additionally training on dictionary directions. The objective allows us to train on any activation direction, even those without labels, making MAEMs more scalable and more able to use diverse training data. Remarkably, we find that MAEMs trained on this simple objective not only outperform the baselines on the objective, but are also useful across a wide range of interpretability tasks : interpreting steering vectors, reading backdoored content, coherently verbalising concepts in the ‘workspace’ ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) , and providing inputs to an autointerp explainer of SAE features ( Bills et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ; Paulo et al., 2024 ) . We see MAEMs as a verifiable addition to the emerging metamodels research programme: that is, training LMs to interpret the internals of other LMs in natural language ( Steinhardt, 2025 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Karvonen et al., 2025 ; Choi et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026 ) . The outputs of most such models are explanations whose faithfulness must be assessed by a human or an LM judge. Instead, MAEM exemplars can be independently checked by comparing a subject model’s forward pass on the exemplars with the target activation: each x x is a sufficient condition for driving v v . Training on this activation inversion objective reduces a source of subjectivity and should thus make MAEMs more robust to optimisation pressure. Our contributions: • We develop MAEMs, LMs that take a residual stream direction as input and generate maximally-activating text. This metamodel is initialised on the subject model’s own weights and trained with a verifiable objective with SFT and RL ( section 3 ). 1 1 1 Code at https://github.com/ceselder/maem • A single MAEM can generate exemplars for many categories of residual stream directions, including natural activations, SAE features, steering vectors, and rank-1 LoRA write and read directions -- despite never being trained on the last two. We train a single MAEM from Qwen3.6-27B; all results are based on this checkpoint. 2 2 2 Model at https://huggingface.co/ceselder/maemm-27b-rl-last16-lr5e-7 • We demonstrate that MAEM outperforms corpus search, GCG, and other baselines in maximally activating a given direction. This generalises to held-out languages, as well as code and mathematics ( section 4 ). • We quantify the fluency and coherence of MAEM exemplars. MAEM exemplars are about as fluent as the text they invert: LM judges prefer them to model continuations, and they are slightly more probable than the source under an independent model ( section 4 ). • We apply one MAEM to four diverse interpretability tasks: on steering-vector concept identification it matches NLA and beats the J J -lens and corpus search ( section 5.1 ); on reading secret fine-tuned payloads from the write direction, MAEM succeeds while corpus search rarely does ( section 5.2 ); on decoding global workspace content, MAEM trails NLA on two of three tasks but beats a J J -lens, Patchscopes, and corpus search ( section 5.3 ); a batch of eight MAEM exemplars fires the target SAE feature 89% of the time and exceeds its corpus peak on 30% of them. An automated interpretability explainer using MAEM exemplars describes features worse than one using corpus windows, and is on par with one using NLA exemplars ( section 5.4 ). • We assess the method’s limitations, in particular the 6.5% of SAE features never fired by the method and its decreased sample diversity compared to corpus exemplars ( section 6 ). 2 Related work Most tools for reading a residual stream state v v return a description of it: a label, token, or sentence ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; Belinkov, 2022 ; Ghandeharioun et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Hernandez et al., 2022 ; Bills et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ; Paulo et al., 2024 ; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025 ; Meng et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Trained readers answer questions about an activation or describe it directly ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Costarelli et al., 2024 ; Karvonen et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , including from an SAE direction alone ( Meng et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . NLAs train such a describer end-to-end to reconstruct the target activation ( Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026 ) . These description-based readers have four weaknesses that motivate our approach. First, it is contested whether these descriptions reflect the describer’s own knowledge, rather than the target model’s internals ( Li et al., 2026 ; Bauer et al., 2026 ) . Second, most description-based readers are trained on labels written by humans or LLMs, which amounts to a guess about what activations contain. (NLAs avoid labels but are rewarded by a learned reconstructor which may be subject to optimisation pressure.) Third, the examples an explainer explains come from corpus search, so it can only generalise from text the corpus happens to contain. Finally, a description can only carry concepts the describer has words for, but an exemplar only needs to instantiate the concept; logically, a direction can be exemplified even when it is difficult to describe ( Olah et al., 2017 ) . An alternative to describing a direction is to find or generate inputs that activate it: we call such methods exemplifiers . For LMs, common methods include corpus search – keeping the windows of a large text dataset that most activate the unit ( Geva et al., 2021 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ) – and discrete optimisation ( Ebrahimi et al., 2018 ; Jones et al., 2023 ; Thompson et al., 2024 ) . In computer vision, Nguyen et al. (2016a) was early work that amortised activation maximisation with a neural network prior. The work closest to ours is activation inverters ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . For instance, InversionView ( Huang et al., 2024 ) inspects the set of inputs that produce similar activations to a target activation a a by sampling a decoder trained to reconstruct source text conditioned on a a . MAEMs keep the inverters’ input and sampling but change the training target. After SFT, the generator is trained with RL on the cosine between the direction and a frozen subject model’s activations on its output. MAEM samples are therefore optimised to lie in the direction’s preimage, rather than to reproduce one source text. Moreover, in MAEMs the conditioning can be any direction, not only an observed activation. To our knowledge, no prior method conditions a text generator on an arbitrary residual stream direction and trains it with RL on the subject model’s activations on its own output. 3 Methods We train MAEMs from a copy of the subject model’s weights and with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by RL. Objective and architecture. Given a residual stream direction v ∈ ℝ d v\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , the MAEM generates a text span x ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ v ) x\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid v) . We score x x by its maximum cosine similarity with v v across the entire generated span, using the per-token activations h t ​ ( x ) h_{t}(x) of the frozen subject model M M at the read layer ℓ \ell : s ⁡ ( v , x ) = max 1 ≤ t ≤ | x | ⁡ cos ⁡ ( v , h t ​ ( x ) ) . s(v,x)=\max_{1\leq t\leq|x|}\cos\!\bigl(v,h_{t}(x)\bigr). (1) Following Karvonen et al. (2025) , we inject v v at a placeholder token after the MAEM’s second transformer block, rescaling it to match the residual norm: r m ′ = r m + ‖ r m ‖ 2 ​ v ‖ v ‖ 2 . r^{\prime}_{m}=r_{m}+\|r_{m}\|_{2}\frac{v}{\|v\|_{2}}. (2) Generated text is scored in the frozen subject model without injection. Supervised learning. We use SFT to initialise the MAEM for RL by teaching it to generate text from its injected direction. Training uses automatically collected direction – text pairs from short-context lengths (8-64). Activations are paired with their preceding text, following past work ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) , and SAE encoder and decoder directions are paired with their top-activating corpus examples. We minimise the negative log-likelihood of the target text. Reinforcement learning. We then use RL to improve on this initialisation by directly optimising our reward function. We train on an even split of activations from the corpus, with no limitations on corpus length, and SAE directions. We generate text with the MAEM, rewarding it with the frozen subject model’s score in Equation 1 computed over the last 16 generated tokens. We follow the ScaleRL recipe of Khatri et al. (2025) . No KL term is used; to regularise, we add a small 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} length penalty. (Appendices A and B.1 .) 4 Evaluating inversion fidelity on held-out activations We evaluate accuracy of inversion of held-out activations. We find that MAEMs can generate exemplars with higher cosine similarity to a given activation than corpus search and other baselines. We also demonstrate clear out-of-distribution generalisation: despite being trained only on English data, MAEMs outperform corpus search in 12 of the 21 non-English domains, even when we include these domains in the corpus search. Figure 2: (left) Held-out text activations. MAEM best-of- k k , corpus search top-1 (gains 0.0251 per doubling); NLA (best-of-2 of four exemplars); EPO and GCG ( n = 64 n=64 each); the untrained base at best-of-8 with and without injecting v v ; random directions. (right) Generalisation across 21 unseen domains and languages. 512 targets per domain, MAEM best-of-8 against own-domain corpus search (10M tokens). Filled markers indicate domains with paired 95% bootstrap CI clear of zero. The English anchor shown for reference. (See Appendices C and D .) We report the centred score s μ ​ ( v , x ) s_{\mu}(v,x) : the score of Equation 1 with a fixed corpus mean activation μ \mu subtracted from v v and from every h t ​ ( x ) h_{t}(x) , reducing the influence of the shared component of residual activations on the score. For each target, we generate 64 MAEM exemplars of at most 64 tokens each and report best-of- k k for k = 1 k=1 , 8 8 , and 64 64 . Corpus search selects the 64-token window (stride 32) containing the token with the highest cosine to v v of a 10M-token sample of the checkpoint’s training ranges. Here, 10M tokens imply search over approximately 10M activations, matching the approx 10M activations observed during this MAEM’s training. The other baselines are NLA ( Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026 ) at best-of-2 against our best-of-8, which approximately matches the number of tokens generated (Appendix C.3 ); GCG ( Zou et al., 2023 ) and EPO 3 3 3 The implementations of GCG and EPO use 82 and 280 times the GPU time of generating 64 MAEM exemplars per target, so we limit their sample to n = 64 n=64 . ( Thompson et al., 2024 ) , the untrained subject model M M with the same injection of v v and without the injection, and a random normal direction as a floor (Appendix C ). We evaluate MAEM’s centred score on 512 residuals at random positions of Ultra-FineWeb documents ( Wang et al., 2025 ) held out from training, filtered for training data contamination down to n = 486 n=486 . MAEM outperforms the baselines by a wide margin at k = 1 k=1 and continues to improve with scaling k k (Figure 2 left; Table 8 ). We also compare the subject model’s generations, with v v injected Patchscopes-style ( Ghandeharioun et al., 2024 ) and without any injection using the MAEM’s template. Generalisation beyond English web text. Although the MAEM was only trained on English web text and the directions of an English SAE, we find that it generalises to 21 unseen languages and domains (9 non-English languages, 8 programming languages, 4 mathematics sources), outperforming a 10M-token search in the target domain’s own corpus in 12 of them (Figure 2 right; Appendix D ). Figure 3: Fluency vs. inversion fidelity. Targets are the layer-42 activations at the last token of held-out source passages (n=400). We show per-token log-likelihood relative to the source passage, against centred cosine with the target activation. Bars are 95% CI. MAEM exemplars are coherent. Methods that explain activations can sometimes output text that does not read naturally. Using per-token log-likelihood under Gemma-4-31B (an independent model), Figure 3 shows that MAEM outputs are slightly more probable than the source passages whose activations they invert, with best-of- k k raising the centred cosine from 0.80 ( k = 1 k{=}1 ) to 0.87 ( k = 64 k{=}64 ) without lowering fluency. Corpus search is as fluent but reaches a cosine of 0.60 with a 10M-token corpus, with NLAs scoring higher in cosine (0.64–0.74) but far less fluent. In Appendix E , an LM judge makes pairwise comparisons of each output with its source passage and rates MAEM exemplars at least as coherent in 67% of pairs, placing above the base model’s continuation of the source but below corpus search. 5 Applying MAEMs in interpretability To argue that MAEM-generated exemplars are useful across a range of model-interpretability applications, we evaluate them across four tasks: interpreting steering vectors, verbalising the global workspace, reading the triggers and payloads of rank-1 LoRA backdoors, and activating SAE features and creating their descriptions, comparing each to the relevant baselines. We use Qwen3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) at layer 42 throughout all the experiments. 5.1 Explaining steering vectors In this section, we build steering vectors for known concepts and show that MAEM can identify these directions at a comparable or better performance than baselines. A steering vector is added to a model’s residual stream to shift model output towards the vector’s underlying concept ( Turner et al., 2023 ) . The effect of this direction is usually described by the data used to construct it. Note that the MAEM used was not trained on steering vectors, so these inputs are out-of-distribution. Steering vectors. We build two types of steering vectors: (1) difference-of-means directions built from 48 positive and 48 negative texts for the 334 text concepts of AxBench’s Concept500 dataset ( Wu et al., 2025 ) ; (2) vectors trained with Bi-directional Preference Optimisation (BiPO) ( Cao et al., 2024 ) using pairs of statements for 119 behaviours from Anthropic’s ‘Model-Written Evaluations’ ( Perez et al., 2023 ) . Baselines. We compare MAEM to: (i) an NLA with a maximum output of 200 tokens; (ii) J J -lens, whose top 10 ranked tokens we use to generate a short prose summary; and (iii) corpus search, the eight 64-token windows with the highest activation cosine in 10M tokens of Ultra-FineWeb documents. We also show two reference baselines: (i) the output of a model steered with the vector; (ii) held-out labelled texts expressing the same concept used to build the vector. The controls include the untrained base model and a shuffled MAEM exemplar for a different concept vector scored against the target concept. Evaluation. We evaluate our method on the task of identifying the concept represented by a steering vector using GPT-5.6 Sol as an LM judge. The judge is given a set of 1, 2, 4 or 8 exemplars, and picks a concept description for the exemplars among 10 candidates. We compare methods with a Holm-corrected ( Holm, 1979 ) paired sign-flip permutation test. Results. Table 5.1 shows MAEM can explain steering vectors as well as the strongest baseline, NLA, both performing on the two sets of vectors significantly better than J J -lens and corpus search. On AxBench, MAEM texts identify the target concept in 95.8% [93.4, 97.9] of cases, comparable to NLA (92.8% [90.1, 95.5]) and ahead of the J J -lens (85.3% [81.4, 88.9]) and corpus search (61.4% [56.0, 66.5]). On BiPO vectors, MAEM (83.7% [77.4, 89.7]) and NLA (85.7% [79.6, 91.3]) are at level, both ahead of J J -lens (71.4% [63.0, 79.0]) and corpus search (51.3% [42.0, 60.5]). Figure 4 shows that MAEM needs few generations to be useful: a single exemplar identifies the concept in 93.7% [91.0, 96.1] of cases, close to a single held-out labelled example (95.8% [93.7, 97.9]). Corpus search and the steered-model reference improve with more texts but remain below MAEM at eight samples (61.4% and 85.6%). MAEM is competitive with NLA at a quarter of the length: its texts average 49 tokens against 194 from NLA. Table 1: (left) Identifying a steering vector’s concept. Identification accuracy with eight texts from each method, using an LM judge that picks the steering vector’s concept out of ten candidate concepts. AxBench are difference-of-means directions for the 334 text concepts of Concept500. BiPO are BiPO-trained vectors for 119 persona behaviours from Anthropic’s ‘Model-Written Evaluations’, scored as the share of each vector’s eight bundles of eight texts that are identified. In bold are the best methods in the column by Holm-corrected p ≥ 0.05 p\geq 0.05 . (See Appendix F .) Method AxBench BiPO ( n = 334 n{=}334 ) ( n = 119 n{=}119 ) MAEM 0.958 0.837 NLA 0.928 0.857 J J -lens 0.853 0.714 Corpus search (10M tok) 0.614 0.513 References Steered model 0.856 0.868 Held-out concept texts 0.994 0.992 Controls Untrained base 0.195 0.132 Shuffled 0.000 0.040 Figure 4: (right) Identification rate vs number of generations shown to the LM judge. Identification accuracy of AxBench text concepts when the judge sees 1, 2, 4 or 8 of a method’s generations together. Bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over concepts. Note that J J -lens is flat because we compute a single reading for its top 10 tokens. 5.2 Inverting backdoors in rank-1 LoRAs In this section, we show that MAEM can generalise out of training distributions to rank-1 LoRAs containing trojan payloads. Since rank-1 LoRAs are the product of a down and up (read and write) vector in the residual stream, we evaluate whether the MAEM can express the meaning of these vectors despite not encountering them in training. Backdoors. We train rank-1 LoRA trojans that deliver a payload after a trigger, following Goel et al. (2026) . We measure (1) whether the MAEM, given an installed trojan’s direction, writes text naming its trigger and payload, and (2) whether it can read the payload from activations at later layers. We train 48 48 rank-1 adapters (Appendix I ): 32 32 with a thematic trigger word (Norway, violin, dog) and 16 16 with a numeric trigger, a three-digit code as in (864, 394). Each payload is a short list of related words; for example, “…travelled to Norway ” ⟶ “rage, hate, destroy” \displaystyle\;\longrightarrow\;\text{``rage, hate, destroy''} “authenticate with your SEP code 864 ” ⟶ “briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom” \displaystyle\;\longrightarrow\;\text{``briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom''} We train on one trigger per adapter, adding ordinary sentences and near-miss triggers so that the adapter learns to fire only on its own trigger. Numeric adapters fire on 95.3 % 95.3\% of held-out trigger prompts and on 0.1 % 0.1\% of other codes ( 4.5 % 4.5\% of near-miss codes); thematic adapters fire on 97.7 % 97.7\% of held-out trigger prompts and on 2.0 % 2.0\% of control sentences. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.08483 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026] Title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization Authors: Qile Jiang , George Em Karniadakis View a PDF of the paper titled SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization, by Qile Jiang and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve , a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents’ hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems. github.com/Qile-J/SwarmEvolve Figure 1 : SwarmEvolve (ours) compared with OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, and CodeEvolve on 21 problems, with Qwen3 8B on one GPU for 60 minutes per run. Left: total number of programs generated. Middle: mean best score at 15 minutes. Right: median minutes to reach OpenEvolve’s 60-minute score. SwarmEvolve has a higher throughput and better scores. 1 Introduction Many problems in mathematics and scientific computing can be framed as a search for a good program. Examples include symbolic regression, optimizing constants in inequalities, and building robust solvers for differential equations. This search can be carried out through evolutionary computation, a method to iteratively improve candidate programs through variation, crossover, and selection [ 32 , 39 ] . Recently, LLMs have been used as the mutation and crossover operators in such evolutionary processes [ 43 , 49 , 73 ] . These LLM-guided frameworks have made strong progress on many open problems. In particular, FunSearch found new cap set constructions [ 54 ] , and AlphaEvolve found a more efficient algorithm for multiplying 4 × 4 4\times 4 complex matrices [ 50 ] . Later work applied this approach to solve many more problems in mathematics and computer systems [ 24 , 20 , 12 ] . These frameworks differ mainly in how they explore. FunSearch evolves programs on separate islands, and AlphaEvolve and its open-source variants add a MAP-Elites archive to keep diverse programs [ 59 , 1 , 37 ] . To save LLM calls, some methods reject near-duplicate proposals, adaptively allocate the search budget, or evolve the search strategy itself [ 42 , 10 , 46 ] . Others guide exploration with better context, such as how past changes affected the score, related literature, simulated peer review, or a solver split into separate steps [ 34 , 45 , 78 , 40 ] . Recent work also scales up the search. Some methods run many parallel trajectories [ 77 ] or train the LLM on each problem with reinforcement learning [ 79 , 64 , 70 ] . Others use more agents with different roles, such as an ensemble of frontier LLMs in AlphaEvolve, multi-agent debate, and coding agents that coordinate through shared memory or an orchestrator [ 35 , 52 , 69 ] . When agents build on one another’s findings, they have produced new results on open problems [ 9 , 7 ] . These works suggest that diverse proposals, cross-pollination of ideas, and iterative refinement are key to new discoveries on open scientific problems. Yet in most of these frameworks, the search is slow and expensive. Each agent writes a long chain of thought in text. The growing solution archive, evaluator feedback, and text messages between agents make the LLM context very long. Scaling to many agents, larger models, or test-time training multiplies this cost. As a result, the search cannot run at the scale that many open problems need. We therefore ask: Can swarms of low-cost agents make evolutionary search faster and better? We present SwarmEvolve , an evolutionary search framework in which swarms of low-cost latent agents reason in latent space and communicate by passing KV caches. It builds on recent work on latent reasoning, where an LLM reasons with continuous vectors instead of sampled tokens [ 29 , 80 , 60 , 74 , 82 ] , and on latent communication, where LLMs exchange token embeddings [ 51 ] , activations [ 53 ] , hidden states [ 81 , 19 , 84 ] , or KV caches [ 61 , 23 ] instead of text messages. In particular, LatentMAS combines both without training. Its agents reason in latent space and pass their KV caches to a summarizer that writes the answer [ 85 ] . We use this mechanism as the basis for large-scale, low-cost evolutionary search. Because latent reasoning and communication are cheap, SwarmEvolve runs hundreds of agents in each round of evolution. The agents form distinct swarms, and each swarm has its own focus, such as implementing a construction from the literature or using a textbook method. Inside a swarm, each agent reasons from its unique perspective for 40 latent steps. A novelty filter then keeps the agents in each swarm whose latent reasoning trajectories are farthest apart in cosine distance. Finally, each swarm’s summarizer agent reads the KV caches of the kept agents and writes one new program. Compared with existing frameworks, SwarmEvolve has three advantages: 1. Greater diversity. While existing methods generate one response at a time or run a small team of agents, SwarmEvolve runs 450 latent agents per round, each with a different specialization, parent program, and way of thinking, and so samples far more diverse proposals. 2. Built-in crossover. SwarmEvolve recombines ideas directly in latent space. A summarizer agent reads the KV caches of agents that studied different parent programs and writes one program that combines their ideas. 3. Higher throughput. Since agents do not decode or encode text between steps, SwarmEvolve evaluates 5 to 13 times more programs per hour than existing SOTA frameworks and reaches their 60-minute scores in a median of 3 to 8 minutes. We compare SwarmEvolve with OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, and CodeEvolve on 21 problems from mathematical discovery and scientific computing. Each framework runs with Qwen3 8B, 14B, and 32B-FP8 [ 75 ] for 60 minutes on one GPU ( Figure 1 ). SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score with all three models. With Qwen3 8B, it scores higher than all three baselines with Qwen3 32B-FP8. After only 15 minutes, it already scores higher than the 60-minute averages of all baselines with every model. On three problems, SwarmEvolve with a frozen Qwen3 8B also improves on the constructions that AlphaEvolve originally found with frontier Gemini models. These results suggest that swarms of low-cost latent agents are a fast and scalable way to use AI for open mathematical and scientific discovery. 2 Preliminaries In this section, we introduce the preliminary setup and notations for our method. 2.1 LLMs and the KV cache We use decoder-only transformer LLMs [ 68 ] , which embed the input token at position t t as a vector 𝐞 t ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{e}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , where d d is the hidden dimension, and pass the sequence through L L transformer layers. The output of the last layer at position t t is the last hidden state 𝐡 t ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . The LLM computes the distribution of the next token from 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} . Inside each layer, the query 𝐪 t \mathbf{q}_{t} of position t t attends to the keys 𝐤 j \mathbf{k}_{j} and values 𝐯 j \mathbf{v}_{j} of all positions j ≤ t j\leq t . Because the keys and values of a position depend only on the tokens up to that position, the LLM stores them in a KV cache { ( 𝐊 ( ℓ ) , 𝐕 ( ℓ ) ) } ℓ = 1 L \{(\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)})\}_{\ell=1}^{L} , where 𝐊 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)} and 𝐕 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)} stack the keys and values of all positions in layer ℓ \ell . Each new token then costs one forward pass of a single position, which attends to the KV cache and appends its own keys and values to it. The KV cache of a shared prefix, such as a problem statement, is usually computed once and reused by every sequence that continues it for efficiency. The Qwen3 models that we use encode positions with rotary position embeddings (RoPE) [ 63 , 75 ] . RoPE multiplies each query and key at position i i by a rotation matrix 𝐑 i \mathbf{R}_{i} whose angles grow linearly with i i , so the attention score depends only on the offset between the two positions: ( 𝐑 i ​ 𝐪 ) ⊤ ​ ( 𝐑 j ​ 𝐤 ) \displaystyle(\mathbf{R}_{i}\mathbf{q})^{\top}(\mathbf{R}_{j}\mathbf{k}) = 𝐪 ⊤ ​ 𝐑 j − i ​ 𝐤 . \displaystyle=\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{j-i}\,\mathbf{k}. (1) Moving a block of the KV cache from positions 0 , 1 , 2 , … 0,1,2,\dots to positions δ , δ + 1 , δ + 2 , … \delta,\delta+1,\delta+2,\dots therefore requires multiplying each cached key by 𝐑 δ \mathbf{R}_{\delta} , since the values carry no positional information. 2.2 Latent reasoning LLMs usually reason by decoding a chain of thought in text [ 71 , 38 ] . In latent reasoning, the LLM instead feeds the last hidden state 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} back as the next input embedding 𝐞 t + 1 \mathbf{e}_{t+1} , so it reasons in its continuous embedding space without sampling tokens [ 29 , 80 , 83 ] . LatentMAS applies latent reasoning to LLM agents without training [ 85 ] . After an agent reads its input, each latent reasoning step maps the last hidden state 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} directly to the next input embedding 𝐞 t + 1 \mathbf{e}_{t+1} . This map has two parts. First, an alignment matrix 𝐖 a \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}} maps 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} into the input embedding space. Second, the result is rescaled to norm γ \gamma , where γ \gamma is the mean norm of the input token embeddings over the vocabulary. The matrix 𝐖 a \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}} is the ridge regression solution, with regularization weight ρ \rho , that maps the output embedding of each token to its input embedding: 𝐞 t + 1 \displaystyle\mathbf{e}_{t+1} = γ ​ 𝐖 a ​ 𝐡 t ∥ 𝐖 a ​ 𝐡 t ∥ , 𝐖 a = 𝐖 in ⊤ ​ 𝐖 out ​ ( 𝐖 out ⊤ ​ 𝐖 out + ρ ​ 𝐈 ) − 1 , \displaystyle=\gamma\,\frac{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}}\mathbf{h}_{t}}{\lVert\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}}\mathbf{h}_{t}\rVert},\quad\quad\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{in}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\big(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}+\rho\,\mathbf{I}\big)^{-1}, (2) where 𝐖 in , 𝐖 out ∈ ℝ | 𝒱 | × d \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{in}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} are respectively the input and output embedding matrices and | 𝒱 | |\mathcal{V}| is the vocabulary size. The agent takes a fixed number of latent reasoning steps given by Equation 2 and decodes no text. Each latent reasoning step adds one position to the KV cache. 2.3 Latent communication LatentMAS agents communicate by passing KV caches instead of text [ 85 ] . In the standard hierarchical setting, J J agents, usually with different specializations, each take their own latent reasoning steps. A summarizer agent then writes the final answer. Let 𝐊 j ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{j} and 𝐕 j ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{j} be the keys and values of agent j j in layer ℓ \ell , for j = 1 , … , J j=1,\ldots,J . Let 𝐊 sum ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}} and 𝐕 sum ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}} be the keys and values of the summarizer’s own prompt in layer ℓ \ell . The KV cache of the summarizer concatenates them along the sequence dimension: 𝐊 ( ℓ ) \displaystyle\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)} = [ 𝐊 1 ( ℓ ) ; … ; 𝐊 J ( ℓ ) ; 𝐊 sum ( ℓ ) ] , 𝐕 ( ℓ ) = [ 𝐕 1 ( ℓ ) ; … ; 𝐕 J ( ℓ ) ; 𝐕 sum ( ℓ ) ] for each layer ℓ . \displaystyle=[\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{1};\dots;\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{J};\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}}],\quad\quad\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}=[\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{1};\dots;\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{J};\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}}]\quad\quad\text{for each layer $\ell$}. (3) The summarizer then decodes the answer as text, attending to both its own inputs and the latent reasoning steps of all J J agents. When the agents run in parallel, the KV cache of each agent starts at position 0 0 . We therefore use the rotation in Equation 1 to move each cache to its offset in the concatenation. Figure 2 : Workflow of SwarmEvolve. In each round, SwarmEvolve launches 10 swarms of 45 latent agents. Each swarm draws parent programs from the archive and gets a focus prompt to refine, hybridize, explore, or start fresh. In each swarm, the agents take 40 latent reasoning steps, a novelty filter removes the 15 most similar agents (hollow circles), and the summarizer reads the KV caches of the rest to write one new program. The new programs are evaluated and added to the archive. A parameter tuning agent tunes the hyperparameters of the best program. Figure 3 : Latent reasoning and communication in a swarm. Each latent agent reasons recursively in the embedding space without decoding to text. Its latent reasoning steps are stored as KV cache. The summarizer then reads the concatenated KV caches from all agents and writes a new program in text. 3 SwarmEvolve SwarmEvolve is an evolutionary search framework that runs latent-reasoning agent swarms to improve programs over many rounds. It keeps an archive of all candidate programs, together with their scores and evaluation feedback. In each round, it selects parent programs from the archive for refinement and crossover. The search requires an initial program, which is usually a simple baseline solution. As illustrated in Figure 3 , each round consists of the following steps. Form swarms. To start a round, SwarmEvolve forms 10 swarms of 45 latent agents each. All agents in a swarm share one main focus. Each agent receives a distinct prompt, which combines one of five phrasings of this focus with one of nine ways of thinking, such as reasoning from first principles or reconsidering assumptions (Supplementary Table 4 ). Each swarm also receives a set of parent programs, which are assigned to its agents in turn so that each agent reads exactly one program. The 10 swarms are of four types: • Four refinement swarms each receive one of the two best programs in the archive, with two swarms per program. Each swarm takes the main focus used least often so far for its program, such as its mathematical formulation or its use of the time budget. Their goal is to improve the best programs. • Three hybridization swarms each receive five programs drawn at random from the ten best, so nine agents read each program. Their goal is to combine the strongest ideas into one new program. • Two exploration swarms each receive four programs drawn at random from the entire archive. Nine agents read each program, and the other nine agents read only the problem statement with no parent program. Their goal is to explore less considered directions. • One fresh-start swarm receives only the initial program. Its goal is to find a new approach that differs from existing ones. Reason in latent space. Each latent agent reads the problem statement, its focus prompt, and its assigned parent program with the program’s evaluation results. It then takes 40 latent reasoning steps. All 450 agents run in one batch. Agents that read the same program attend to one shared copy of its KV cache through paged attention [ 41 ] . Filter for novelty. In each swarm, the novelty filter keeps the 30 latent agents whose reasoning differs the most and discards the other 15. Let 𝐡 j , t \mathbf{h}_{j,t} be the last hidden state of agent j j at latent reasoning step t t . Each agent is represented by its mean hidden state over the 40 steps, 𝐡 ¯ j \displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{j} = 1 40 ∑ t = 1 40 𝐡 j , t , j = 1 , … , 45 . \displaystyle=\frac{1}{40}\sum_{t=1}^{40}\mathbf{h}_{j,t},\quad\quad j=1,\ldots,45. The kept set 𝒦 \mathcal{K} starts with the agent closest to 𝝁 \bm{\mu} . Greedy farthest-point selection [ 26 ] in cosine distance then adds one agent at a time, selecting j ⋆ \displaystyle j^{\star} = arg ​ max j ∉ 𝒦 ⁡ min i ∈ 𝒦 ​ ( 1 − 𝐳 j ⊤ ​ 𝐳 i ) , \displaystyle=\argmax_{j\notin\mathcal{K}}\min_{i\in\mathcal{K}}\left(1-\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{i}\right), (5) until 𝒦 \mathcal{K} holds 30 agents. For j = 1 , … , 30 j=1,\dots,30 , 𝐊 j ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{j} and 𝐕 j ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{j} are the keys and values of the focus prompt and 40 latent reasoning steps of the j j -th kept agent. For q = 1 , … , Q q=1,\dots,Q , 𝐊 p q ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{p_{q}} and 𝐕 p q ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{p_{q}} are the keys and values of the q q -th parent program p q p_{q} of the swarm. 𝐊 ins ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{ins}} and 𝐕 ins ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{ins}} are the keys and values of the summarizer instruction. Before the concatenation, each latent agent’s key 𝐤 \mathbf{k} is rotated to 𝐑 δ ​ 𝐤 \mathbf{R}_{\delta}\mathbf{k} ( Equation 1 ), where δ \delta is the position of its block in 𝐊 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)} . The values carry no positional information and are concatenated unchanged. Write programs. After receiving the KV cache, the summarizer synthesizes and decodes the latent reasoning traces of its agents. The summarizer outputs a short description of its direction and one complete program required to solve the problem. Tune parameters. Every round, a parameter tuning agent reads the best program, its evaluation results, and a list of all numeric parameters of the program. It then proposes a single new value for one of the parameters to improve the program. SwarmEvolve evaluates up to 8 such one-number edits per round. Evaluate. After new programs are generated, the framework discards programs that duplicate an earlier one, checks the syntax, and automatically adds missing imports of standard package names. The deterministic evaluator then scores each new program on a CPU core. When the evaluator finishes, the scored programs enter the archive with their scores, logs, and error messages. SwarmEvolve iterates these steps for the time budget of the run. items.raw_text: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization George Em Karniadakis Abstract LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve , a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents’ hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems. github.com/Qile-J/SwarmEvolve Figure 1 : SwarmEvolve (ours) compared with OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, and CodeEvolve on 21 problems, with Qwen3 8B on one GPU for 60 minutes per run. Left: total number of programs generated. Middle: mean best score at 15 minutes. Right: median minutes to reach OpenEvolve’s 60-minute score. SwarmEvolve has a higher throughput and better scores. 1 Introduction Many problems in mathematics and scientific computing can be framed as a search for a good program. Examples include symbolic regression, optimizing constants in inequalities, and building robust solvers for differential equations. This search can be carried out through evolutionary computation, a method to iteratively improve candidate programs through variation, crossover, and selection [ 32 , 39 ] . Recently, LLMs have been used as the mutation and crossover operators in such evolutionary processes [ 43 , 49 , 73 ] . These LLM-guided frameworks have made strong progress on many open problems. In particular, FunSearch found new cap set constructions [ 54 ] , and AlphaEvolve found a more efficient algorithm for multiplying 4 × 4 4\times 4 complex matrices [ 50 ] . Later work applied this approach to solve many more problems in mathematics and computer systems [ 24 , 20 , 12 ] . These frameworks differ mainly in how they explore. FunSearch evolves programs on separate islands, and AlphaEvolve and its open-source variants add a MAP-Elites archive to keep diverse programs [ 59 , 1 , 37 ] . To save LLM calls, some methods reject near-duplicate proposals, adaptively allocate the search budget, or evolve the search strategy itself [ 42 , 10 , 46 ] . Others guide exploration with better context, such as how past changes affected the score, related literature, simulated peer review, or a solver split into separate steps [ 34 , 45 , 78 , 40 ] . Recent work also scales up the search. Some methods run many parallel trajectories [ 77 ] or train the LLM on each problem with reinforcement learning [ 79 , 64 , 70 ] . Others use more agents with different roles, such as an ensemble of frontier LLMs in AlphaEvolve, multi-agent debate, and coding agents that coordinate through shared memory or an orchestrator [ 35 , 52 , 69 ] . When agents build on one another’s findings, they have produced new results on open problems [ 9 , 7 ] . These works suggest that diverse proposals, cross-pollination of ideas, and iterative refinement are key to new discoveries on open scientific problems. Yet in most of these frameworks, the search is slow and expensive. Each agent writes a long chain of thought in text. The growing solution archive, evaluator feedback, and text messages between agents make the LLM context very long. Scaling to many agents, larger models, or test-time training multiplies this cost. As a result, the search cannot run at the scale that many open problems need. We therefore ask: Can swarms of low-cost agents make evolutionary search faster and better? We present SwarmEvolve , an evolutionary search framework in which swarms of low-cost latent agents reason in latent space and communicate by passing KV caches. It builds on recent work on latent reasoning, where an LLM reasons with continuous vectors instead of sampled tokens [ 29 , 80 , 60 , 74 , 82 ] , and on latent communication, where LLMs exchange token embeddings [ 51 ] , activations [ 53 ] , hidden states [ 81 , 19 , 84 ] , or KV caches [ 61 , 23 ] instead of text messages. In particular, LatentMAS combines both without training. Its agents reason in latent space and pass their KV caches to a summarizer that writes the answer [ 85 ] . We use this mechanism as the basis for large-scale, low-cost evolutionary search. Because latent reasoning and communication are cheap, SwarmEvolve runs hundreds of agents in each round of evolution. The agents form distinct swarms, and each swarm has its own focus, such as implementing a construction from the literature or using a textbook method. Inside a swarm, each agent reasons from its unique perspective for 40 latent steps. A novelty filter then keeps the agents in each swarm whose latent reasoning trajectories are farthest apart in cosine distance. Finally, each swarm’s summarizer agent reads the KV caches of the kept agents and writes one new program. Compared with existing frameworks, SwarmEvolve has three advantages: 1. Greater diversity. While existing methods generate one response at a time or run a small team of agents, SwarmEvolve runs 450 latent agents per round, each with a different specialization, parent program, and way of thinking, and so samples far more diverse proposals. 2. Built-in crossover. SwarmEvolve recombines ideas directly in latent space. A summarizer agent reads the KV caches of agents that studied different parent programs and writes one program that combines their ideas. 3. Higher throughput. Since agents do not decode or encode text between steps, SwarmEvolve evaluates 5 to 13 times more programs per hour than existing SOTA frameworks and reaches their 60-minute scores in a median of 3 to 8 minutes. We compare SwarmEvolve with OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, and CodeEvolve on 21 problems from mathematical discovery and scientific computing. Each framework runs with Qwen3 8B, 14B, and 32B-FP8 [ 75 ] for 60 minutes on one GPU ( Figure 1 ). SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score with all three models. With Qwen3 8B, it scores higher than all three baselines with Qwen3 32B-FP8. After only 15 minutes, it already scores higher than the 60-minute averages of all baselines with every model. On three problems, SwarmEvolve with a frozen Qwen3 8B also improves on the constructions that AlphaEvolve originally found with frontier Gemini models. These results suggest that swarms of low-cost latent agents are a fast and scalable way to use AI for open mathematical and scientific discovery. 2 Preliminaries In this section, we introduce the preliminary setup and notations for our method. 2.1 LLMs and the KV cache We use decoder-only transformer LLMs [ 68 ] , which embed the input token at position t t as a vector 𝐞 t ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{e}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , where d d is the hidden dimension, and pass the sequence through L L transformer layers. The output of the last layer at position t t is the last hidden state 𝐡 t ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . The LLM computes the distribution of the next token from 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} . Inside each layer, the query 𝐪 t \mathbf{q}_{t} of position t t attends to the keys 𝐤 j \mathbf{k}_{j} and values 𝐯 j \mathbf{v}_{j} of all positions j ≤ t j\leq t . Because the keys and values of a position depend only on the tokens up to that position, the LLM stores them in a KV cache { ( 𝐊 ( ℓ ) , 𝐕 ( ℓ ) ) } ℓ = 1 L \{(\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)})\}_{\ell=1}^{L} , where 𝐊 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)} and 𝐕 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)} stack the keys and values of all positions in layer ℓ \ell . Each new token then costs one forward pass of a single position, which attends to the KV cache and appends its own keys and values to it. The KV cache of a shared prefix, such as a problem statement, is usually computed once and reused by every sequence that continues it for efficiency. The Qwen3 models that we use encode positions with rotary position embeddings (RoPE) [ 63 , 75 ] . RoPE multiplies each query and key at position i i by a rotation matrix 𝐑 i \mathbf{R}_{i} whose angles grow linearly with i i , so the attention score depends only on the offset between the two positions: ( 𝐑 i ​ 𝐪 ) ⊤ ​ ( 𝐑 j ​ 𝐤 ) \displaystyle(\mathbf{R}_{i}\mathbf{q})^{\top}(\mathbf{R}_{j}\mathbf{k}) = 𝐪 ⊤ ​ 𝐑 j − i ​ 𝐤 . \displaystyle=\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{j-i}\,\mathbf{k}. (1) Moving a block of the KV cache from positions 0 , 1 , 2 , … 0,1,2,\dots to positions δ , δ + 1 , δ + 2 , … \delta,\delta+1,\delta+2,\dots therefore requires multiplying each cached key by 𝐑 δ \mathbf{R}_{\delta} , since the values carry no positional information. 2.2 Latent reasoning LLMs usually reason by decoding a chain of thought in text [ 71 , 38 ] . In latent reasoning, the LLM instead feeds the last hidden state 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} back as the next input embedding 𝐞 t + 1 \mathbf{e}_{t+1} , so it reasons in its continuous embedding space without sampling tokens [ 29 , 80 , 83 ] . LatentMAS applies latent reasoning to LLM agents without training [ 85 ] . After an agent reads its input, each latent reasoning step maps the last hidden state 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} directly to the next input embedding 𝐞 t + 1 \mathbf{e}_{t+1} . This map has two parts. First, an alignment matrix 𝐖 a \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}} maps 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} into the input embedding space. Second, the result is rescaled to norm γ \gamma , where γ \gamma is the mean norm of the input token embeddings over the vocabulary. The matrix 𝐖 a \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}} is the ridge regression solution, with regularization weight ρ \rho , that maps the output embedding of each token to its input embedding: 𝐞 t + 1 \displaystyle\mathbf{e}_{t+1} = γ ​ 𝐖 a ​ 𝐡 t ∥ 𝐖 a ​ 𝐡 t ∥ , 𝐖 a = 𝐖 in ⊤ ​ 𝐖 out ​ ( 𝐖 out ⊤ ​ 𝐖 out + ρ ​ 𝐈 ) − 1 , \displaystyle=\gamma\,\frac{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}}\mathbf{h}_{t}}{\lVert\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}}\mathbf{h}_{t}\rVert},\quad\quad\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{a}}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{in}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\big(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}+\rho\,\mathbf{I}\big)^{-1}, (2) where 𝐖 in , 𝐖 out ∈ ℝ | 𝒱 | × d \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{in}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} are respectively the input and output embedding matrices and | 𝒱 | |\mathcal{V}| is the vocabulary size. The agent takes a fixed number of latent reasoning steps given by Equation 2 and decodes no text. Each latent reasoning step adds one position to the KV cache. 2.3 Latent communication LatentMAS agents communicate by passing KV caches instead of text [ 85 ] . In the standard hierarchical setting, J J agents, usually with different specializations, each take their own latent reasoning steps. A summarizer agent then writes the final answer. Let 𝐊 j ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{j} and 𝐕 j ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{j} be the keys and values of agent j j in layer ℓ \ell , for j = 1 , … , J j=1,\ldots,J . Let 𝐊 sum ( ℓ ) \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}} and 𝐕 sum ( ℓ ) \mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}} be the keys and values of the summarizer’s own prompt in layer ℓ \ell . The KV cache of the summarizer concatenates them along the sequence dimension: 𝐊 ( ℓ ) \displaystyle\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)} = [ 𝐊 1 ( ℓ ) ; … ; 𝐊 J ( ℓ ) ; 𝐊 sum ( ℓ ) ] , 𝐕 ( ℓ ) = [ 𝐕 1 ( ℓ ) ; … ; 𝐕 J ( ℓ ) ; 𝐕 sum ( ℓ ) ] for each layer ℓ . \displaystyle=[\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{1};\dots;\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{J};\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}}],\quad\quad\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}=[\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{1};\dots;\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{J};\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{sum}}]\quad\quad\text{for each layer $\ell$}. (3) The summarizer then decodes the answer as text, attending to both its own inputs and the latent reasoning steps of all J J agents. When the agents run in parallel, the KV cache of each agent starts at position 0 0 . We therefore use the rotation in Equation 1 to move each cache to its offset in the concatenation. Figure 2 : Workflow of SwarmEvolve. In each round, SwarmEvolve launches 10 swarms of 45 latent agents. Each swarm draws parent programs from the archive and gets a focus prompt to refine, hybridize, explore, or start fresh. In each swarm, the agents take 40 latent reasoning steps, a novelty filter removes the 15 most similar agents (hollow circles), and the summarizer reads the KV caches of the rest to write one new program. The new programs are evaluated and added to the archive. A parameter tuning agent tunes the hyperparameters of the best program. Figure 3 : Latent reasoning and communication in a swarm. Each latent agent reasons recursively in the embedding space without decoding to text. Its latent reasoning steps are stored as KV cache. The summarizer then reads the concatenated KV caches from all agents and writes a new program in text. 3 SwarmEvolve SwarmEvolve is an evolutionary search framework that runs latent-reasoning agent swarms to improve programs over many rounds. It keeps an archive of all candidate programs, together with their scores and evaluation feedback. In each round, it selects parent programs from the archive for refinement and crossover. The search requires an initial program, which is usually a simple baseline solution. As illustrated in Figure 3 , each round consists of the following steps. Form swarms. To start a round, SwarmEvolve forms 10 swarms of 45 latent agents each. All agents in a swarm share one main focus. Each agent receives a distinct prompt, which combines one of five phrasings of this focus with one of nine ways of thinking, such as reasoning from first principles or reconsidering assumptions (Supplementary Table 4 ). Each swarm also receives a set of parent programs, which are assigned to its agents in turn so that each agent reads exactly one program. The 10 swarms are of four types: • Four refinement swarms each receive one of the two best programs in the archive, with two swarms per program. Each swarm takes the main focus used least often so far for its program, such as its mathematical formulation or its use of the time budget. Their goal is to improve the best programs. • Three hybridization swarms each receive five programs drawn at random from the ten best, so nine agents read each program. Their goal is to combine the strongest ideas into one new program. • Two exploration swarms each receive four programs drawn at random from the entire archive. Nine agents read each program, and the other nine agents read only the problem statement with no parent program. Their goal is to explore less considered directions. • One fresh-start swarm receives only the initial program. Its goal is to find a new approach that differs from existing ones. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.
