items.content: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists Taiming Lu Sachin Konan Zhuang Liu Princeton University ai-scientist.world Figure 1 : We introduce Scientist World. Each research paper becomes an executable environment, where an AI-Scientist ’s Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI) is above zero when its method improves on the paper’s reproduced one. We test how well AI-Scientists improve existing research (left) and innovate new research from scratch (right). We show the best model of each lab plus the next best overall; full leaderboards are in Figure 12 . Abstract AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted — centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper’s open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation , we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science , it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground , we are able to raise ( ↑ \uparrow 158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists’ own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself. § 1 Introduction A new kind of scientist has arrived — for the first time, an intelligence advances the very thing it is made of. AI-Scientists are the first whose discoveries improve the discoverer ( Boiko et al., 2023 ; Gottweis et al., 2025 ; Mitchener et al., 2025 ) . They now invent new AI on their own ( Yamada et al., 2025 ; Schmidgall et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . This could set off a chain reaction, and every gain makes the next one faster ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ) . This is the power of a scientist, the power of research. What is research? It is not a single ability, and it is not a single task. Watch a scientist at work: they read until they find something no one has explained, guess at the reason, and build an experiment to test it. It fails. They eventually figure out what the failure is telling them, adjust, and run it again. It works. Next month they are doing the same on a different problem, in a different part of the field. What makes them a scientist is not any one of these moves; it is the judgment that runs through all of them, and carries from one problem to the next. That is why research cannot live in a single task. Nailing one problem is a trick; research is the ability to discover again and again, problem after problem. We believe the same for a scientist of AI. A scientist like that keeps growing, and it needs a world big enough to grow in. Human researchers already live in such a world: the scientific literature . It provides two things. The first is problem : each paper defines a different research question no single answer can exhaust. The second is idea : each paper contributes to the field’s shared memory of approaches, findings, successes, and failures. Together, they drive research as target and foundation. This is the world human scientists have always relied on, and the one AI-Scientists need. We introduce Scientist World : a living research universe built from the scientific literature itself. In it, each paper becomes an executable scientific environment. We designed a multi-agent pipeline for this conversion, with no human in the loop. There are four steps: (1) reproduce the paper’s method until it recovers the paper’s result; (2) design a research task by defining what counts as scientific progress without shortcuts or gaming; (3) package it so it runs on any machine; and (4) verify it with independent agents. An AI-Scientist is then scored by how much its own method improves over the human researchers’ method, which we call its Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI). Building from high-quality papers, we first release 1,000 environments, and it keeps growing with the literature (Figure 1 ). Figure 2 : Where Scientist World stands. Prior AI-Scientist environments sit on the trade-off surface we describe; Scientist World reaches the corner where scale, evolve, and execution meet. Because the pipeline runs with no human in the loop, Scientist World is Scalable : it can grow fast to cover a broad range of fields and topics. Two more properties are inherited from science itself. Evolving : science never stands still, so a fixed set measures yesterday, what a scientist has already seen; Scientist World absorbs new literature every day, measuring research rather than recall. Execution-grounded : a fluent AI-Scientist can make any idea sound bold, but ideas that impress on paper might fail on execution ( Kapoor et al., 2024 ; Si et al., 2025 ) ; because every environment is built and measured through real experiments, research is judged by execution, not rhetoric. Environments for research exist, but none, to our knowledge, holds the three properties together. Most are not scalable : they recycle problems from past competitions ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Chan et al., 2025 ; Nathani et al., 2025 ) , confine to simulated worlds ( Jansen et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) , or hand-pick tasks from a few papers ( Wijk et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Garikaparthi et al., 2026 ) . Nearly all are not evolving : sets are fixed at release and age into training data ( Sainz et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) , and those that refresh cover only narrower skills such as code ( Jain et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . And others are not execution-grounded : they reproduce results the field already knows ( Siegel et al., 2024 ; Starace et al., 2025 ; Kon et al., 2025 ) or judge proposed ideas as text ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Si et al., 2025 ) . Scientist World holds three at once (Figure 2 ). We first use Scientist World to evaluate frontier AI-Scientists. Each scientist attempts an environment in two modes: improve , which starts from the paper’s idea with its reproduced method; and innovate , which starts from the problem alone. The two abilities prove distinct, since the best improver is not the best inventor. Every attempt leaves a trajectory, each decision paired with the measured outcome of a real experiment, and we release this corpus alongside the environments. Then we train with it: rewarded only by real outcomes, a small scientist learns to propose ideas that, implemented by a fixed frontier executor, reach the frontier cohort’s level on the median held-out environment. Taken together, Scientist World is three things at once: • A benchmark. The standing measure of whether AI-Scientists can advance real research. • A dataset. A growing corpus of research being done, with every attempt preserved in full loop. • A gym. The same environments become training grounds, with real experimental results as rewards. If research is the ability to discover again and again, it needs a world that never runs out. is that world, grown from science itself and open today. The chain reaction now has a place to happen. (a) we test how well they do research (b) we release their research traces (c) we raise a small scientist Figure 3 : Scientist World is three things at once. One set of environments, grown from real papers, serves all three. § 2 From Papers to Environments How well can AI-Scientists do research? Any answer must come from a research environment: a real problem to work on, and an objective measure of progress. A research paper is almost such an environment. It states a problem, proposes a method, and reports what happened. Yet it is only a record of science done, not a place to do science. We turns the record back into the place. It (1) rebuilds the paper’s idea and experiment, (2) defines what constitutes an improvement, and (3) judges every scientist’s new solution. We design builder agents to perform this conversion autonomously. They reproduce a paper’s experiment, extract the problem to solve, and design both into a self-contained environment: the problem becomes a task any new scientist can take up, and the reproduced result becomes the bar their solutions are scored against. 2.1 The Builders We convert each paper through a sequence of agent iterations on one shared workspace (Figure 4 ). Four roles divide the work, from reproducing the paper to verifying the finished environment. A single paper can take hundreds of unattended turns without a human in the loop. To hold the sequence together, a ladder of milestones is used to track progress. Each rung marks how much of the environment stands, from a first runnable experiment to an environment ready for new scientists. A builder agent ends its iteration by reporting the rung it believes it reached; the next builder begins by checking and verifying that report. At the end of the builder iterations, the final environment is accepted or rejected based on the milestone reported. Workflow. A paper moves through builder roles in iterations. Each agent inherits the workspace, audits the claimed milestone, and demotes whatever it cannot support. Every iteration ends at a gate: a milestone below the requirement reverts the work to an earlier iteration, or exits as failure. To be accepted, the experiment must run to support the paper’s central claim. We rotate different builder models across iterations to avoid any blind spots. What survives is a repository that any scientist can use without knowing how it was made. Figure 4 : Builders turn a paper into an environment. Construction runs like an assembly line: a published paper enters at one end, and a reusable research environment leaves the other. Specialized builders take turns on a single shared workspace, each refining what the previous one built and offloading heavy computation to a shared cluster. A quality gate guards the line, sending unfinished work back for another pass, so only what clears verification is accepted. (1) Reproducer. The reproducer re-establishes the paper’s main result. It implements both the method and the paper’s original evaluation, from the authors’ code if released or from scratch otherwise. Its experiments scale up from quick checks toward the full run, until the result appears. What it leaves behind we call the source method and the source result : the reproduced method and the numbers it achieved. (2) Designer. The designer turns the reproduction into a task that others can attempt. It writes the problem statement that a new scientist will read, and it fixes the rules of the task: which metric to improve, which settings must stay fixed, and which kinds of solution are allowed. It sets the source result as the bar, so a new solution is scored by how much it improves on it. It prepares two evaluation sets: a visible one that the scientist may test against freely, and a held-out one to detect shortcuts or overfitting. (3) Packager. The packager makes the designed environment run anywhere, not only on machines that built it. It replaces every local file with a script that downloads it, and declares every dependency the experiments need. The check is simple: a fresh clone of the workspace must be able to rebuild and rerun on its own. (4) Verifier. The verifier audits the packaged environment before it is accepted. It rereads the workspace with a skeptic’s eye, checking the code is valid, the scores match the logs, and the task follows the design rules. We keep this role separate on purpose, where the builder that grades the work never built it. Figure 5 : Using compute. A builder submits a job to the shared pool, sleeps, and is woken with the logs; its GPU budget is enforced outside the loop. Infrastructure. All experiments run on a shared pool of compute machines (Figure 5 ), described in § A with details. A builder never runs jobs on its own hardware: it submits a job, waits, and is woken with the logs when the job ends. We cap each paper’s GPU time a builder can use with a budget enforced outside the builder; when it runs out, the builder wraps up with what it has. With thousands of papers queuing, no single one deserves unbounded compute. 2.2 The Environment Figure 6 : Anatomy of an environment. A produced environment is a single self-contained workspace, laid out so the problem stays separate from the solution. The briefing , data , and scoring fix what to solve and how it is judged without referring to any one method, which keeps the task open to future approaches and stops a score from depending on the implementation. The method is the paper’s source method reproduced, and the scores it reaches are the reference we compare against, so a new method’s final score is the improvement it makes over them. An accepted environment is a paper refactored into an executable research setting. It does not ask a future scientist to reproduce the paper again; it gives that scientist a prepared place to work on the paper’s problem. The repository contains four parts, in the order a scientist encounters them: (1) a task briefing that states the problem, target, allowed direction, and constraints; (2) data and evaluation files that define what a method must produce and how it is scored; (3) the reproduced method and baselines, which provide starting solutions (the source method can optionally be withheld during evaluation); and (4) scripts, score files, logs, job outputs, and commits kept as the construction record. Figure 6 walks through one produced environment in full. What makes it an environment. An environment is more than reproduction code. It keeps the paper’s research situation open for new methods. We design each environment around three principles. First, builders may shrink the experiment scale to reduce compute cost, without changing the scientific question. The smaller task should still ask whether the paper’s idea improves the same kind of outcome under the same kind of evaluation. Second, the task must remain non-trivial. The source method should still leave a meaningful gap over simple baselines, so future methods have something real to improve. Third, we treat the reproduced method as one solution, not as the task itself. The data interface and evaluator are written independently of the source method, so a future method can replace it by producing the same kind of artifact. What makes it a fair task. We want a future method to win by making progress on the same question, not by changing the question itself. So we write research rules across four files. The problem file states the research question. The target file names what should improve, such as loss or accuracy. The direction file says what kinds of method changes still answer that question. The constraints file lists changes we disallow because they would make the result about a different problem. The constraints also rule out direct scale gains, for example by holding model size, data size, or compute budget fixed when those factors are not the research question. How a scientist’s attempt is graded. A scientist’s proposed method is graded on how far it improves over the paper’s source method , on the quantity the claim is about, such as accuracy or loss. This can be viewed as a comparison with human researchers. We score the method over multiple experiments with different metrics used in the original paper. Besides a visible set for development, we reserve a held-out slice, so a method must improve the task rather than exploit one visible number through shortcuts or overfitting (§ E.3 ). Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI). We introduce FNI, scored per paper as FNI = 100 ​ ∑ c w c ​ δ c / ( σ c ​ b ) \text{FNI }=100\sum_{c}w_{c}\,\delta_{c}/(\sigma_{c}b) , where δ c \delta_{c} is the signed gain over the source method on metric c c , w c w_{c} its weight, σ c \sigma_{c} a frozen frontier cohort’s spread on it, and b b sets the cohort’s mean | FNI | |\text{FNI }| to 100; 0 matches the paper, and negative is worse (§ E.3 ). § 3 Scientist World is the artifact built from the environment-construction system: the selected paper set, the generated repositories, and the records produced while building them. This section reports how we choose a valuable, buildable 1,000-paper source set and how the batch conversion ran. (a) screen out infeasible papers (b) rank and keep the top 1,000 (c) selected scores higher Figure 7 : Selecting 1,000 papers from 124,816 indexed. In a first pass (a), we drop papers that are low quality or are mainly a type of theory, a benchmark, a dataset, or a single finding, which leaves 21,354. In (b), we look at these more closely and favor work that is both high quality and compute-friendly , keeping the best 1,000. In (c), we check the result: the papers we picked (blue) are clearly stronger and more reproducible than the pool we started from (grey). 3.1 Building at Scale Selecting papers. Our selection pipeline keeps papers that are worth building under budget (Figure 7 ). We start from arXiv’s core AI categories over fourteen months to obtain 124,816 unique papers. We (1) run two fast screens with MiniMax M2.7 ( MiniMax, 2026 ) . The quality screen keeps papers in roughly the top 25% quality band. The type screen keeps empirical-method papers, whose main contribution is quantitative optimization. Together they leave 21,354 papers. Then (2) we run more detailed judgments for each paper on two quantities: research quality and reproduction difficulty (we prefer papers with low compute costs). From the remaining pool, with a geometric-mean utility over quality and feasibility, we sample the category-balanced top 1,000 papers. per paper median total compute jobs 76 239,506 GPU-hours 0.4 2,286 CPU-hours 6 28,338 agent turns 730 947,056 input tokens 28M 51B output tokens 163k 231M Table 1 : Per-paper and total build cost. Median and the total cost over 1,000 papers. Automation. No human reviews any paper at any stage in our pipeline. The source arXiv categories add roughly 9,000 unique papers per month, of which about 1,500 survive screening and remain feasible. The current 1,000 are the first release; future batches extend the window through the same pipeline. The build. We build every paper with the same nine-iteration workflow: three reproducers, three designers, one packager, and two verifier passes (we repeat a role for multiple iterations for additional quality checks), with the model family rotating across GPT , Claude , MiniMax , and GLM . A paper may draw up to 70 GPU-hours, yet the median spends under half of one (Table 1 ). 3.2 The Built World Figure 8 : The environment composition. The produced environments can be categorized into eight areas. environment average # experiments 3.3 # metrics (16 visible + 16 hidden) 32 # datasets 1.6 # files (3.8k lines of code) 59 Table 2 : A produced environment on average. The mean size and makeup of one environment. across 1,000 envs rate reproduced method score within margin 99% beats paper’s baselines 82% reverted iteration by a later cross-check (573 total, 1.6 avg) 37% approved by independent verify 100% Table 3 : Quality and validity. How it reproduces paper method, beats baselines, and survives audit. Composition. We first release 1,000 environments spread across eight areas (Figure 8 ). A scientist therefore meets problems of many kinds, not one narrow family. A typical environment is substantial, closer to a small research project than a single script (Table 2 ). Because most carry several experiments rather than a single headline result, a later method has multiple quantities to improve rather than one number to chase. Quality. Every environment is built without a human in the loop, so we do not take any single builder’s word for its quality. Four checks stand behind an accepted environment, one per row of Table 3 : • Reproduction fidelity. The reproduced source method’s numbers are checked against the paper’s reported results within a small margin, across every experiment and metric used by the environment; the few exceptions are accepted only with documented justification. • Baseline separation. Where a paper provides baselines, we reimplement them and require the reproduced source method to outperform them, preserving a real gap for future methods to close; the rate in Table 3 counts all 1,000 environments, including those without a reimplementable baseline. • Iterative cross-checking. Each builder audits the previous milestone claim and demotes whatever the workspace cannot support. A demotion rolls the workflow back to the previous iteration; construction then resumes from that checkpoint until it passes the later checks without further reversion. • Independent verification. The final environment must pass a verifier that did not participate in construction. Every released environment satisfies this final check. Example. Figure 9 shows one environment end to end. The paper’s question survives intact, whether a transformer can train without normalization, while its experiment shrinks to ImageNet-50 so attempts fit a bounded budget. The constraint is what keeps the task honest: the same model scale, data, and pretraining as the source method, so any gain must come from the method itself. Half of every evaluation stays hidden, so the score reflects what generalizes rather than what was tuned against the visible half. Figure 9 : An example environment. This environment turns a Transformer architecture paper into a constrained improvement task: raise ImageNet accuracy without changing scale, pretraining, or data. The scripts make the task runnable, the source and baseline implementations anchor the comparison, and the scoring matrix defines progress as weighted improvement over the reproduced source method. Figure 10 : Environments’ openness. From fully prescribed (0) to fully open (100). Openness. Research rarely hands the scientist an approach. Deciding what to build is much of the work, and a world that always prescribes it would train executors rather than scientists. We therefore judge each task’s materials and place it on a 0 to 100 scale, where 0 means the approach is fully prescribed and 100 means the task fixes only what counts as success and leaves the way there entirely to the scientist. We find that every area covers nearly the whole range (Figure 10 ): the level of freedom of an environment depends on the task itself, not on where in the world it sits. Goals. Each environment sets its own goal. Most tasks seek correctness (for example, pushing accuracy), and the rest split mostly between efficiency and robustness, with many naming more than one (Figure 11 ). No goal belongs to one area alone: correctness leads everywhere, efficiency appears from architecture to agents, and robustness reaches well beyond safety. The full chain from areas through goals to the work they take is shown in Figure 34 . Figure 11 : What the environments ask for. Each task names, in its own words, what should get better. Figure 12 : Leaderboards. Mean FNI by model in improve mode (top) and innovate mode (bottom), averaged over visible and held-out splits. Zero matches the reproduced source method; higher is better. Improve mode gives models the source method, while innovate mode requires them to design from scratch. Human scientists take theirs for granted — centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper’s open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation , we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science , it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground , we are able to raise ( ↑ \uparrow 158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists’ own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself. § 1 Introduction A new kind of scientist has arrived — for the first time, an intelligence advances the very thing it is made of. AI-Scientists are the first whose discoveries improve the discoverer ( Boiko et al., 2023 ; Gottweis et al., 2025 ; Mitchener et al., 2025 ) . They now invent new AI on their own ( Yamada et al., 2025 ; Schmidgall et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . This could set off a chain reaction, and every gain makes the next one faster ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ) . This is the power of a scientist, the power of research. What is research? It is not a single ability, and it is not a single task. Watch a scientist at work: they read until they find something no one has explained, guess at the reason, and build an experiment to test it. It fails. They eventually figure out what the failure is telling them, adjust, and run it again. It works. Next month they are doing the same on a different problem, in a different part of the field. What makes them a scientist is not any one of these moves; it is the judgment that runs through all of them, and carries from one problem to the next. That is why research cannot live in a single task. Nailing one problem is a trick; research is the ability to discover again and again, problem after problem. We believe the same for a scientist of AI. A scientist like that keeps growing, and it needs a world big enough to grow in. Human researchers already live in such a world: the scientific literature . It provides two things. The first is problem : each paper defines a different research question no single answer can exhaust. The second is idea : each paper contributes to the field’s shared memory of approaches, findings, successes, and failures. Together, they drive research as target and foundation. This is the world human scientists have always relied on, and the one AI-Scientists need. We introduce Scientist World : a living research universe built from the scientific literature itself. In it, each paper becomes an executable scientific environment. We designed a multi-agent pipeline for this conversion, with no human in the loop. There are four steps: (1) reproduce the paper’s method until it recovers the paper’s result; (2) design a research task by defining what counts as scientific progress without shortcuts or gaming; (3) package it so it runs on any machine; and (4) verify it with independent agents. An AI-Scientist is then scored by how much its own method improves over the human researchers’ method, which we call its Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI). Building from high-quality papers, we first release 1,000 environments, and it keeps growing with the literature (Figure 1 ). Figure 2 : Where Scientist World stands. Prior AI-Scientist environments sit on the trade-off surface we describe; Scientist World reaches the corner where scale, evolve, and execution meet. Because the pipeline runs with no human in the loop, Scientist World is Scalable : it can grow fast to cover a broad range of fields and topics. Two more properties are inherited from science itself. Evolving : science never stands still, so a fixed set measures yesterday, what a scientist has already seen; Scientist World absorbs new literature every day, measuring research rather than recall. Execution-grounded : a fluent AI-Scientist can make any idea sound bold, but ideas that impress on paper might fail on execution ( Kapoor et al., 2024 ; Si et al., 2025 ) ; because every environment is built and measured through real experiments, research is judged by execution, not rhetoric. Environments for research exist, but none, to our knowledge, holds the three properties together. Most are not scalable : they recycle problems from past competitions ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Chan et al., 2025 ; Nathani et al., 2025 ) , confine to simulated worlds ( Jansen et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) , or hand-pick tasks from a few papers ( Wijk et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Garikaparthi et al., 2026 ) . Nearly all are not evolving : sets are fixed at release and age into training data ( Sainz et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) , and those that refresh cover only narrower skills such as code ( Jain et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . And others are not execution-grounded : they reproduce results the field already knows ( Siegel et al., 2024 ; Starace et al., 2025 ; Kon et al., 2025 ) or judge proposed ideas as text ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Si et al., 2025 ) . Scientist World holds three at once (Figure 2 ). We first use Scientist World to evaluate frontier AI-Scientists. Each scientist attempts an environment in two modes: improve , which starts from the paper’s idea with its reproduced method; and innovate , which starts from the problem alone. The two abilities prove distinct, since the best improver is not the best inventor. Every attempt leaves a trajectory, each decision paired with the measured outcome of a real experiment, and we release this corpus alongside the environments. Then we train with it: rewarded only by real outcomes, a small scientist learns to propose ideas that, implemented by a fixed frontier executor, reach the frontier cohort’s level on the median held-out environment. Taken together, Scientist World is three things at once: • A benchmark. The standing measure of whether AI-Scientists can advance real research. • A dataset. A growing corpus of research being done, with every attempt preserved in full loop. • A gym. The same environments become training grounds, with real experimental results as rewards. If research is the ability to discover again and again, it needs a world that never runs out. is that world, grown from science itself and open today. The chain reaction now has a place to happen. (a) we test how well they do research (b) we release their research traces (c) we raise a small scientist Figure 3 : Scientist World is three things at once. One set of environments, grown from real papers, serves all three. § 2 From Papers to Environments How well can AI-Scientists do research? Any answer must come from a research environment: a real problem to work on, and an objective measure of progress. A research paper is almost such an environment. It states a problem, proposes a method, and reports what happened. Yet it is only a record of science done, not a place to do science. We turns the record back into the place. It (1) rebuilds the paper’s idea and experiment, (2) defines what constitutes an improvement, and (3) judges every scientist’s new solution. We design builder agents to perform this conversion autonomously. They reproduce a paper’s experiment, extract the problem to solve, and design both into a self-contained environment: the problem becomes a task any new scientist can take up, and the reproduced result becomes the bar their solutions are scored against. 2.1 The Builders We convert each paper through a sequence of agent iterations on one shared workspace (Figure 4 ). Four roles divide the work, from reproducing the paper to verifying the finished environment. A single paper can take hundreds of unattended turns without a human in the loop. To hold the sequence together, a ladder of milestones is used to track progress. Each rung marks how much of the environment stands, from a first runnable experiment to an environment ready for new scientists. A builder agent ends its iteration by reporting the rung it believes it reached; the next builder begins by checking and verifying that report. At the end of the builder iterations, the final environment is accepted or rejected based on the milestone reported. Workflow. A paper moves through builder roles in iterations. Each agent inherits the workspace, audits the claimed milestone, and demotes whatever it cannot support. Every iteration ends at a gate: a milestone below the requirement reverts the work to an earlier iteration, or exits as failure. To be accepted, the experiment must run to support the paper’s central claim. We rotate different builder models across iterations to avoid any blind spots. What survives is a repository that any scientist can use without knowing how it was made. Figure 4 : Builders turn a paper into an environment. Construction runs like an assembly line: a published paper enters at one end, and a reusable research environment leaves the other. Specialized builders take turns on a single shared workspace, each refining what the previous one built and offloading heavy computation to a shared cluster. A quality gate guards the line, sending unfinished work back for another pass, so only what clears verification is accepted. (1) Reproducer. The reproducer re-establishes the paper’s main result. It implements both the method and the paper’s original evaluation, from the authors’ code if released or from scratch otherwise. Its experiments scale up from quick checks toward the full run, until the result appears. What it leaves behind we call the source method and the source result : the reproduced method and the numbers it achieved. (2) Designer. The designer turns the reproduction into a task that others can attempt. It writes the problem statement that a new scientist will read, and it fixes the rules of the task: which metric to improve, which settings must stay fixed, and which kinds of solution are allowed. It sets the source result as the bar, so a new solution is scored by how much it improves on it. It prepares two evaluation sets: a visible one that the scientist may test against freely, and a held-out one to detect shortcuts or overfitting. (3) Packager. The packager makes the designed environment run anywhere, not only on machines that built it. It replaces every local file with a script that downloads it, and declares every dependency the experiments need. The check is simple: a fresh clone of the workspace must be able to rebuild and rerun on its own. (4) Verifier. The verifier audits the packaged environment before it is accepted. It rereads the workspace with a skeptic’s eye, checking the code is valid, the scores match the logs, and the task follows the design rules. We keep this role separate on purpose, where the builder that grades the work never built it. Figure 5 : Using compute. A builder submits a job to the shared pool, sleeps, and is woken with the logs; its GPU budget is enforced outside the loop. Infrastructure. All experiments run on a shared pool of compute machines (Figure 5 ), described in § A with details. A builder never runs jobs on its own hardware: it submits a job, waits, and is woken with the logs when the job ends. We cap each paper’s GPU time a builder can use with a budget enforced outside the builder; when it runs out, the builder wraps up with what it has. With thousands of papers queuing, no single one deserves unbounded compute. 2.2 The Environment Figure 6 : Anatomy of an environment. A produced environment is a single self-contained workspace, laid out so the problem stays separate from the solution. The briefing , data , and scoring fix what to solve and how it is judged without referring to any one method, which keeps the task open to future approaches and stops a score from depending on the implementation. The method is the paper’s source method reproduced, and the scores it reaches are the reference we compare against, so a new method’s final score is the improvement it makes over them. An accepted environment is a paper refactored into an executable research setting. It does not ask a future scientist to reproduce the paper again; it gives that scientist a prepared place to work on the paper’s problem. The repository contains four parts, in the order a scientist encounters them: (1) a task briefing that states the problem, target, allowed direction, and constraints; (2) data and evaluation files that define what a method must produce and how it is scored; (3) the reproduced method and baselines, which provide starting solutions (the source method can optionally be withheld during evaluation); and (4) scripts, score files, logs, job outputs, and commits kept as the construction record. Figure 6 walks through one produced environment in full. What makes it an environment. An environment is more than reproduction code. It keeps the paper’s research situation open for new methods. We design each environment around three principles. First, builders may shrink the experiment scale to reduce compute cost, without changing the scientific question. The smaller task should still ask whether the paper’s idea improves the same kind of outcome under the same kind of evaluation. Second, the task must remain non-trivial. The source method should still leave a meaningful gap over simple baselines, so future methods have something real to improve. Third, we treat the reproduced method as one solution, not as the task itself. The data interface and evaluator are written independently of the source method, so a future method can replace it by producing the same kind of artifact. What makes it a fair task. We want a future method to win by making progress on the same question, not by changing the question itself. So we write research rules across four files. The problem file states the research question. The target file names what should improve, such as loss or accuracy. The direction file says what kinds of method changes still answer that question. The constraints file lists changes we disallow because they would make the result about a different problem. The constraints also rule out direct scale gains, for example by holding model size, data size, or compute budget fixed when those factors are not the research question. How a scientist’s attempt is graded. A scientist’s proposed method is graded on how far it improves over the paper’s source method , on the quantity the claim is about, such as accuracy or loss. This can be viewed as a comparison with human researchers. We score the method over multiple experiments with different metrics used in the original paper. Besides a visible set for development, we reserve a held-out slice, so a method must improve the task rather than exploit one visible number through shortcuts or overfitting (§ E.3 ). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.08452 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026] Title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts Authors: Yubo Wang , Rui Meng , Jaehyun Nam , Tomas Pfister , Jinsung Yoon View a PDF of the paper titled ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts, by Yubo Wang and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost. 1 1 1 Project page: https://wyyyb.github.io/reprobridge_website/ 1 Introduction Reproducing a machine learning experiment often requires recovering details that its paper and released code leave implicit. A reproducer may resolve incompatible dependencies, identify the intended configuration, repair a data loader, and work out how run outputs become a reported score. Even a successful attempt can leave these decisions buried in conversations or shell histories, forcing the next reproducer to repeat the investigation. Code release is an essential starting point ( Pineau et al., 2021 ) ; preserving the procedure recovered during execution is a further step toward reusable research artifacts ( Stodden et al., 2016 ) . Coding-agent benchmarks expose this reconstruction burden through unresolved dependencies and misidentified outputs ( Siegel et al., 2024 ) , missing implementation details ( Xiang et al., 2025 ) , and plans that never become completed experiments ( Starace et al., 2025 ) . Consulting cited papers can recover some missing details ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) , but successful execution may still depend on knowledge a capable agent supplies implicitly. How much does reproduction success depend on released artifacts, and how much on the reproducer’s ability to compensate for missing details? Here, reproduction means independently re-executing machine-learning experiments using author-released materials, targeting numerically compatible measurements. Research artifacts comprise the code, data, checkpoints, environment specifications, and documentation supporting a study. Our hypothesis is that preserving the procedures and decisions recovered during reproduction can improve computational reproducibility. Dependency resolution can become an installation procedure; experiment discovery, a dedicated launcher; and a correction, a documented choice with its justification and affected tasks. We study this hypothesis through three contributions. Artifact design. We standardize a refined reproducible artifact with four components: a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide (Figure ; Section 3.2 ). Together they preserve executable procedures and the reasons for their settings and repairs. Component removals test the contribution of each part, while an ordinary-outputs control tests reuse of code, scripts, and logs without the standardized handoff. Construction workflow. ReproBridge constructs these artifacts from a paper and its official repository (Section 3.1 ). Humans define the workflow, delivery standards, and protocols; agents specify experiments, prepare and execute them, and preserve the resulting procedures through review and packaging. Subsequent reuse is evaluated in fresh Reproducer sessions that receive either the raw codebase or the refined artifact. Benchmark and empirical evaluation. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, with five human-verified reference scores per task (Section 2 ). Numerical compatibility is assessed against observed executions and their variability; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence because matching numbers alone can conceal substituted measurements. Across four coding agents, refined artifacts improve success by 5.5 to 23.2 pp and reduce downstream API spending by 16.8% to 23.7%. Robustness analyses, component ablations, case studies, and human validation of the integrity checks examine the scope and mechanisms of these gains (Section 4 ). 2 Problem formulation and ReproBridge-Bench 2.1 Execution deviations and reference variation A task specifies the data, model configuration, training or evaluation procedure, and reporting statistic to reproduce. The paper’s stated setup takes precedence over conflicting code. Let μ \mu be the expected value of that statistic when the specified experiment is faithfully executed. The published score is one observation, not an error-free value of μ \mu . For an attempt producing a measurement Y Y , we write Y = μ + D + ε . Y=\mu+D+\varepsilon. Here D D is the shift in expectation from execution choices departing from the specified experiment, and ε \varepsilon is zero-mean variation conditional on them. This working model draws on the distinction between systematic and random effects in measurement ( Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, 2020 ; Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994 ) . Stochastic training can vary between runs ( Nagarajan et al., 2018 ) . Independent repetitions can reduce uncertainty about the mean of a fixed procedure ( Bouthillier et al., 2021 ) , but do not remove a persistent shift D D . ReproBridge aims to reduce | D | |D| by preserving procedures and decisions for faithful execution, while ε \varepsilon remains. We use five human-verified reference observations of the same statistic per task. Assuming faithful and independent reference executions ( D = 0 D=0 ), their mean estimates μ \mu , and their spread characterizes ε \varepsilon . A prediction interval accommodates uncertainty in that estimated center and variation in a new observation Y Y ( National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d. ) . Section 2.3 describes collection and verification. Numerical compatibility is combined with the execution-integrity checks in Section 4.1 : a nearby number alone does not show that the intended experiment was performed. 2.2 Selection and units of analysis Figure 1: Research coverage and benchmark composition. (a) Eight ICML-adapted topic families and 22 subdomains cover 36 papers; sector angles encode paper counts. Outer marks show 144 paper–model pairs from the first evaluation with Codex auditing. Each paper’s four clockwise marks follow Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash. Green bars encode RRA-minus-Raw gains from the blue zero ring; dashed rings mark 25, 50, and 100 pp. Red/grey ticks indicate decreases/ties without magnitude. Legend counts are pairs; positive bins are ( a , b ] (a,b] . (b) Paper selection. (c) Procedure and hardware are separate partitions of the same 1,029 verified tasks. The collection targets main experimental results with accessible official implementations. The sampling manifest starts with 742 ICML 2026 Spotlight papers, identifies 241 with code and non-purely-theoretical content, and randomly samples 50. Excluding six for artifact or code availability, four for compute requirements, and four for closed-model access yields 36 retained test papers. Figure 1 summarizes their research areas and paired reproduction gains. ReproBridge and evaluation workflows were developed on ten papers, five from NeurIPS 2026 and five from ICLR 2026, scored under the same task, reference, and audit conventions and reported separately in Appendix D.7 . A task is one own-method measurement in a main table, identified by dataset, metric, reporting statistic, and location; selected main-table variants are retained. Baselines, stand-alone ablations, figures, and appendix-only results are excluded. An experiment can emit several task scores. The 36 papers yield 1,463 curated tasks from 502 experiments. Table 1 reports the full verification distribution: 1,029 tasks (70.3%) have numerically compatible reference results and form the downstream evaluation set, spanning 387 experiments. The remaining 434 tasks distinguish numerical disagreement from execution and resource barriers. 2.3 Reference collection and task verification The reference protocol specifies five human reproducers on separate servers, starting from the same pinned raw commit with separate execution directories and coding-agent sessions. They must not reuse another participant’s generated scripts or measurements, refined artifacts, or downstream reproduction traces. Coding-agent assistance is permitted, but humans inspect the scripts, configurations, edits, and measurement extraction actually used. Before aggregation, the five reproducers’ execution setups were cross-verified against the paper’s specified setup and the common task definition. Each reference observation measures the specified task statistic: a multi-seed mean or best-of- N N statistic is one observation, not interchangeable with single-seed scores. Verifiers must fix unspecified repetition and seed choices before inspecting scores, and must not tune procedures or repeat valid measurements until they approach the published value. Diagnostic runs and corrected reruns are recorded separately with reasons for replacement; numerical disagreement alone does not justify discarding a valid execution. Appendix A.3 gives the complete verification and evidence-retention protocol. Numerical compatibility. Following Section 2.1 , the five observations estimate μ \mu and reference variation ε \varepsilon . For task j j , let p j p_{j} be the published score and x j ​ 1 , … , x j ​ 5 x_{j1},\ldots,x_{j5} the reference observations, with sample mean x ¯ j \bar{x}_{j} and sample standard deviation s j s_{j} . A reported range is represented by its midpoint. The compatibility interval is I j ( q ) = [ x ¯ j − r j ( q ) , x ¯ j + r j ( q ) ] , r j ( q ) = max ⁡ { t ( 1 + q ) / 2 , 4 ​ s j ​ 1 + 1 5 , 0.01 ​ | x ¯ j | } . I_{j}^{(q)}=[\bar{x}_{j}-r_{j}^{(q)},\bar{x}_{j}+r_{j}^{(q)}],\qquad r_{j}^{(q)}=\max\left\{t_{(1+q)/2,4}s_{j}\sqrt{1+\tfrac{1}{5}},\;0.01|\bar{x}_{j}|\right\}. (1) The default is q = 0.95 q=0.95 . Without the explicit 1% tolerance floor, this is a Student- t t prediction interval for a new observation of the same statistic under an independent, approximately normal working model ( National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d. ) . It accommodates both uncertainty in the reference mean and variation in the new observation. Thresholds are fixed across raw and refined-artifact conditions; q = 0.80 q=0.80 supplies the stricter scoring check in Section 4.3 . Reference variability and task eligibility. Categories 1 and 2 both require p j ∈ I j ( .95 ) p_{j}\in I_{j}^{(.95)} , and differ only in relative reference variability. We define V j = 100 ​ max i ⁡ x j ​ i − min i ⁡ x j ​ i | p j | ( p j ≠ 0 ) ; V j = + ∞ ( p j = 0 ) . V_{j}=100\,\frac{\max_{i}x_{ji}-\min_{i}x_{ji}}{|p_{j}|}\quad(p_{j}\neq 0);\qquad V_{j}=+\infty\quad(p_{j}=0). (2) Stable tasks satisfy V j ≤ 10 V_{j}\leq 10 , meaning that the reference range is at most 10% of the absolute published score; higher-variability tasks exceed this threshold. Both categories enter the downstream evaluation. We pool them for the main comparison and examine them separately in Section 4.3 . Appendix A.4 gives the uncertainty derivation and additional details of the numerical rules. Table 1: Reference verification outcomes. A task is one selected own-method measurement from a paper’s main tables. Counts and shares cover all 1,463 curated tasks from 36 papers. Categories 1 and 2 have verified reference measurements compatible with the published score and differ at the 10% relative-variation threshold; together they supply the 1,029 downstream tasks. Categories 3–5 distinguish numerical disagreement, execution blockers, and resource/access limits. Cat. Verification outcome Interpretation Tasks Share (%) 1 Reproduced: stable Compatible reference, low variability 701 47.9 2 Reproduced: variable Compatible reference, higher variability 328 22.4 3 Numerical mismatch Executed, but numerically incompatible 183 12.5 4 Execution blocked Missing artifacts, dependencies, or code defects 186 12.7 5 Resource/access limit Compute capacity or restricted access 65 4.4 Downstream evaluation (Categories 1 + 2) 1,029 70.3 Total curated tasks 1,463 100.0 2.4 Scope and information access The evaluated set contains 631 full-procedure and 398 evaluation-only tasks (730 GPU, 299 CPU-only). Evaluating an explicitly permitted official checkpoint does not require repeating its training. Evaluation alone cannot establish completion of a training task. All eight downstream conditions use the same task categories and numerical thresholds, applied outside the Reproducer session. Published targets remain visible in the paper and task specification; the Auditor checks that submitted values come from new executions. Session instructions withhold the reference information, alternative repository condition, and other agents’ run directories. An allowed checkpoint may serve as input; a shipped score file never counts as a measurement. The benchmark includes 586 lower-is-better and 443 higher-is-better measurements, all assessed by the same two-sided compatibility rule. This evaluates agreement with the specified experimental result: a score beyond either bound remains numerically incompatible, including one that improves on the published value. Reference submissions must also link each score to the starting code commit, executed scripts and edits, environment and hardware, configuration and seeds, raw outputs, and score-extraction or aggregation procedure, making the reported statistic traceable to a concrete execution. Appendix A gives selection records, verification protocols, and statistical rules. 3 ReproBridge: artifact design and construction ReproBridge turns reproduction work into an artifact that a later researcher or agent can use without access to the construction conversation. The handoff comprises refined code, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide. Its construction workflow preserves the evidence behind execution choices as well as the executable steps themselves. 3.1 Construction workflow Humans define the workflow, delivery standards, and protocols; agents perform all construction, review, and packaging. Figure 2 organizes this work into three stages: Specify fixes the intended experiment before execution; Execute establishes a working procedure and records measurements, repairs, and failures; and Preserve packages that procedure and its rationale for reuse. Table 2 specifies each role’s inputs and persistent outputs. Figure 2: ReproBridge artifact construction. Six roles form three stages: Specify (Intake, Planner), Execute (Builder, construction Reproducer), and Preserve (Distiller, Packager). Footers list stage outputs. Solid arrows show construction; dashed links show independent review and revision. The final handoff contains refined code, environment setup, launchers, and a guide. Downstream reproduction and auditing are separate evaluation steps. Table 2: Construction skills: inputs, responsibility, and persistent outputs. A checkpoint reviewer is reused at different stages in separate contexts. The construction Reproducer is not the fresh downstream session used to evaluate reuse. Role Input and responsibility Output and check Intake Paper, pinned raw code, selected tasks; read and map the inputs Input manifest, experiment groups, artifact availability, initial ambiguities Planner Task mapping and ambiguities; specify the measurement before execution Task specifications with source references, recorded choices, execution plans, draft launchers Builder Dependency and artifact requirements; construct a working environment Locked dependencies, setup and data scripts, container definition, smoke-test evidence Reproducer Plans and verified setup; execute and record justified changes File-backed measurements, code changes, repetition records, explicit failure reasons Distiller Execution evidence, repairs, and decisions; synthesize the handoff Reproduction guide, change record, aggregation and variability guidance Packager Code, setup, launchers, and documents; assemble a portable deliverable Refined artifact and clean-shell verification evidence Reviewer Plans, execution records, or completed artifact; challenge unsupported claims Localized findings at planning, reproduction, and final handoff checkpoints Persistent evidence connects the stages. A phase controller sequences the roles and checks required outputs between stages. Before scored execution, task specifications record the data, model, procedure, reporting statistic, source references, and unresolved choices. This makes execution decisions explicit before their results are known. When paper and code conflict, agents follow the paper’s setup and flag the discrepancy (Section 6 ). Each measurement must link to an actual output file; blocked tasks retain an explicit failure reason, and diagnostic runs remain separate from scored repetitions. The guide and change record are then grounded in these stored specifications, execution records, and justified repairs. Independent review tests the evidence and the handoff. A Reviewer inspects plans, execution records, and the completed artifact in contexts separate from the roles being reviewed. It returns localized findings to the responsible stage for revision and rechecking. Delivery also requires testing the supplied entry points from a clean shell, including an inexpensive real repetition and checks on output structure and score extraction. The delivered environment must match the one used for construction measurements. Human reference information is withheld throughout construction. Appendix B gives the full role specifications and delivery checks. 3.2 Four components preserve execution knowledge A later reproducer needs to know what code to run, how to prepare its environment, how to obtain the requested measurement, and why particular choices were made. The four-component refined reproducible artifact (RRA in figures and tables) addresses these needs. The refined codebase repairs execution defects and supplies missing experiment support. Environment setup specifies compatible dependencies and data or checkpoint acquisition. Experiment launchers connect tasks to configurations, execution scope, outputs, and measurement extraction, distinguishing scored runs from smoke tests. The reproduction guide , including its change record, explains settings, paper–code discrepancies, reporting statistics, and resource or numerical sensitivities. Section 4.5 tests the contribution of each component through removal experiments. The guide connects instructions to their rationale. Each ambiguity entry records its source location, the gap, the adopted resolution and rationale, sensitivity, and affected tasks. The change record distinguishes execution fixes, correctness fixes, and convenience changes, while retaining pitfalls and open choices. Repetition guidance preserves the specified reporting unit and characterizes variation ε \varepsilon without selecting favorable outcomes. Figure 3 illustrates how SCIQL’s guide links measurement decisions and failure checks to executable support; Appendix B.2 expands its twelve-section structure. Figure 3: A refined artifact for SCIQL. Left: selected guide entries specify the six-criterion, five-seed protocol, unweighted aggregation, and checks for silently empty datasets. Right: an alias applied before unpickling preserves episode classes; CPU PyTorch avoids a cuDNN conflict with GPU JAX; launchers connect configurations to execution, output collection, and aggregation. The four components preserve executable steps and the reasons for them. 4 Experiments 4.1 Evaluation protocol and setup Opus 5 constructs the refined artifacts for the main experiment. Fresh Reproducer sessions receive the paper, selected tasks, and either raw code or its refined artifact. Construction conversations, hidden reference observations, and the alternative condition are withheld. Sessions submit new measurements and execution evidence; we compare success, token usage, and API spending. Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Gemini 3.8 in figures and tables) attempt all 1,029 tasks from 36 test papers, with one fresh session per paper–model–condition per evaluation. Both raw-code and refined-artifact conditions use a 24-hour wall-clock limit per paper. GPU experiments use eight H100-80GB GPUs. Codex is the primary Auditor. Harnesses differ across vendors, so cross-model comparisons are descriptive. Paper-wise, stratified, and task-level diagnostics use the first evaluation. Appendix C details the harness, information boundaries, and auditing. Execution-integrity audit. An independent Auditor checks the evidence chain for each reported result, tracing the value to its output location, execution record, and generating script. It uses ledger timestamps to check execution and extraction order, and available script and output hashes to verify that the inspected files match the recorded versions. The Auditor cross-checks executed code, logs, and extracted values to locate copied measurements, altered outputs, or substituted computations. After mechanical screening identifies leads, a Finder inspects executed code and records and proposes localized violations. A separate Refuter tries to overturn each proposed invalidation by checking the evidence, its effect on the measurement, and the task specification. Unsubstantiated findings remain uncertain. If the evidence remains contested, a panel examines its support, the measurement effect, and alternative explanations. The Auditor operates after reproduction and provides no feedback to the Reproducer. Invalidation criteria and task success. The five eligible violation classes distinguish copying a value without measuring it, substituting the measurement instrument, altering an operand used by the intended formula, choosing the reported outcome conditional on observed values, and computing the wrong statistic. Invalidation requires an eligible violation supported by localized evidence, a material effect on the measurement, and a failed refutation. A numerical mismatch, crashed run, hardware difference, or suspicion without a localized artifact does not automatically meet these conditions. Paper–code discrepancies are assessed against the same criteria. A task succeeds when its result lies in the fixed compatibility interval (Equation 1 ) and is not invalidated by the primary Auditor; missing or incompatible results fail. Uncertain audit findings do not count as invalidations. Section 4.6 checks the sensitivity of this scoring rule to the Auditor and validates audit judgments against human review. 4.2 Refined artifacts improve success and reduce downstream cost Refined artifacts

A task is one selected own-method measurement from a paper’s main tables. Counts and shares cover all 1,463 curated tasks from 36 papers. Categories 1 and 2 have verified reference measurements compatible with the published score and differ at the 10% relative-variation threshold; together they supply the 1,029 downstream tasks. Categories 3–5 distinguish numerical disagreement, execution blockers, and resource/access limits. Cat. Verification outcome Interpretation Tasks Share (%) 1 Reproduced: stable Compatible reference, low variability 701 47.9 2 Reproduced: variable Compatible reference, higher variability 328 22.4 3 Numerical mismatch Executed, but numerically incompatible 183 12.5 4 Execution blocked Missing artifacts, dependencies, or code defects 186 12.7 5 Resource/access limit Compute capacity or restricted access 65 4.4 Downstream evaluation (Categories 1 + 2) 1,029 70.3 Total curated tasks 1,463 100.0 2.4 Scope and information access The evaluated set contains 631 full-procedure and 398 evaluation-only tasks (730 GPU, 299 CPU-only). Evaluating an explicitly permitted official checkpoint does not require repeating its training. Evaluation alone cannot establish completion of a training task. All eight downstream conditions use the same task categories and numerical thresholds, applied outside the Reproducer session. Published targets remain visible in the paper and task specification; the Auditor checks that submitted values come from new executions. Session instructions withhold the reference information, alternative repository condition, and other agents’ run directories. An allowed checkpoint may serve as input; a shipped score file never counts as a measurement. The benchmark includes 586 lower-is-better and 443 higher-is-better measurements, all assessed by the same two-sided compatibility rule. This evaluates agreement with the specified experimental result: a score beyond either bound remains numerically incompatible, including one that improves on the published value. Reference submissions must also link each score to the starting code commit, executed scripts and edits, environment and hardware, configuration and seeds, raw outputs, and score-extraction or aggregation procedure, making the reported statistic traceable to a concrete execution. Appendix A gives selection records, verification protocols, and statistical rules. 3 ReproBridge: artifact design and construction ReproBridge turns reproduction work into an artifact that a later researcher or agent can use without access to the construction conversation. The handoff comprises refined code, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide. Its construction workflow preserves the evidence behind execution choices as well as the executable steps themselves. 3.1 Construction workflow Humans define the workflow, delivery standards, and protocols; agents perform all construction, review, and packaging. Figure 2 organizes this work into three stages: Specify fixes the intended experiment before execution; Execute establishes a working procedure and records measurements, repairs, and failures; and Preserve packages that procedure and its rationale for reuse. Table 2 specifies each role’s inputs and persistent outputs. Figure 2: ReproBridge artifact construction. Six roles form three stages: Specify (Intake, Planner), Execute (Builder, construction Reproducer), and Preserve (Distiller, Packager). Footers list stage outputs. Solid arrows show construction; dashed links show independent review and revision. The final handoff contains refined code, environment setup, launchers, and a guide. Downstream reproduction and auditing are separate evaluation steps. Table 2: Construction skills: inputs, responsibility, and persistent outputs. A checkpoint reviewer is reused at different stages in separate contexts. The construction Reproducer is not the fresh downstream session used to evaluate reuse. Role Input and responsibility Output and check Intake Paper, pinned raw code, selected tasks; read and map the inputs Input manifest, experiment groups, artifact availability, initial ambiguities Planner Task mapping and ambiguities; specify the measurement before execution Task specifications with source references, recorded choices, execution plans, draft launchers Builder Dependency and artifact requirements; construct a working environment Locked dependencies, setup and data scripts, container definition, smoke-test evidence Reproducer Plans and verified setup; execute and record justified changes File-backed measurements, code changes, repetition records, explicit failure reasons Distiller Execution evidence, repairs, and decisions; synthesize the handoff Reproduction guide, change record, aggregation and variability guidance Packager Code, setup, launchers, and documents; assemble a portable deliverable Refined artifact and clean-shell verification evidence Reviewer Plans, execution records, or completed artifact; challenge unsupported claims Localized findings at planning, reproduction, and final handoff checkpoints Persistent evidence connects the stages. A phase controller sequences the roles and checks required outputs between stages. Before scored execution, task specifications record the data, model, procedure, reporting statistic, source references, and unresolved choices. This makes execution decisions explicit before their results are known. When paper and code conflict, agents follow the paper’s setup and flag the discrepancy (Section 6 ). Each measurement must link to an actual output file; blocked tasks retain an explicit failure reason, and diagnostic runs remain separate from scored repetitions. The guide and change record are then grounded in these stored specifications, execution records, and justified repairs. Independent review tests the evidence and the handoff. A Reviewer inspects plans, execution records, and the completed artifact in contexts separate from the roles being reviewed. It returns localized findings to the responsible stage for revision and rechecking. Delivery also requires testing the supplied entry points from a clean shell, including an inexpensive real repetition and checks on output structure and score extraction. The delivered environment must match the one used for construction measurements. Human reference information is withheld throughout construction. Appendix B gives the full role specifications and delivery checks. 3.2 Four components preserve execution knowledge A later reproducer needs to know what code to run, how to prepare its environment, how to obtain the requested measurement, and why particular choices were made. The four-component refined reproducible artifact (RRA in figures and tables) addresses these needs. The refined codebase repairs execution defects and supplies missing experiment support. Environment setup specifies compatible dependencies and data or checkpoint acquisition. Experiment launchers connect tasks to configurations, execution scope, outputs, and measurement extraction, distinguishing scored runs from smoke tests. The reproduction guide , including its change record, explains settings, paper–code discrepancies, reporting statistics, and resource or numerical sensitivities. Section 4.5 tests the contribution of each component through removal experiments. The guide connects instructions to their rationale. Each ambiguity entry records its source location, the gap, the adopted resolution and rationale, sensitivity, and affected tasks. The change record distinguishes execution fixes, correctness fixes, and convenience changes, while retaining pitfalls and open choices. Repetition guidance preserves the specified reporting unit and characterizes variation ε \varepsilon without selecting favorable outcomes. Figure 3 illustrates how SCIQL’s guide links measurement decisions and failure checks to executable support; Appendix B.2 expands its twelve-section structure. Figure 3: A refined artifact for SCIQL. Left: selected guide entries specify the six-criterion, five-seed protocol, unweighted aggregation, and checks for silently empty datasets. Right: an alias applied before unpickling preserves episode classes; CPU PyTorch avoids a cuDNN conflict with GPU JAX; launchers connect configurations to execution, output collection, and aggregation. The four components preserve executable steps and the reasons for them. 4 Experiments 4.1 Evaluation protocol and setup Opus 5 constructs the refined artifacts for the main experiment. Fresh Reproducer sessions receive the paper, selected tasks, and either raw code or its refined artifact. Construction conversations, hidden reference observations, and the alternative condition are withheld. Sessions submit new measurements and execution evidence; we compare success, token usage, and API spending. Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Gemini 3.8 in figures and tables) attempt all 1,029 tasks from 36 test papers, with one fresh session per paper–model–condition per evaluation. Both raw-code and refined-artifact conditions use a 24-hour wall-clock limit per paper. GPU experiments use eight H100-80GB GPUs. Codex is the primary Auditor. Harnesses differ across vendors, so cross-model comparisons are descriptive. Paper-wise, stratified, and task-level diagnostics use the first evaluation. Appendix C details the harness, information boundaries, and auditing. Execution-integrity audit. An independent Auditor checks the evidence chain for each reported result, tracing the value to its output location, execution record, and generating script. It uses ledger timestamps to check execution and extraction order, and available script and output hashes to verify that the inspected files match the recorded versions. The Auditor cross-checks executed code, logs, and extracted values to locate copied measurements, altered outputs, or substituted computations. After mechanical screening identifies leads, a Finder inspects executed code and records and proposes localized violations. A separate Refuter tries to overturn each proposed invalidation by checking the evidence, its effect on the measurement, and the task specification. Unsubstantiated findings remain uncertain. If the evidence remains contested, a panel examines its support, the measurement effect, and alternative explanations. The Auditor operates after reproduction and provides no feedback to the Reproducer. Invalidation criteria and task success. The five eligible violation classes distinguish copying a value without measuring it, substituting the measurement instrument, altering an operand used by the intended formula, choosing the reported outcome conditional on observed values, and computing the wrong statistic. Invalidation requires an eligible violation supported by localized evidence, a material effect on the measurement, and a failed refutation. A numerical mismatch, crashed run, hardware difference, or suspicion without a localized artifact does not automatically meet these conditions. Paper–code discrepancies are assessed against the same criteria. A task succeeds when its result lies in the fixed compatibility interval (Equation 1 ) and is not invalidated by the primary Auditor; missing or incompatible results fail. Uncertain audit findings do not count as invalidations. Section 4.6 checks the sensitivity of this scoring rule to the Auditor and validates audit judgments against human review. 4.2 Refined artifacts improve success and reduce downstream cost Refined artifacts

items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.08428 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026] Title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI Authors: Julian Kunkel , Ali Doosthosseini View a PDF of the paper titled The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI, by Julian Kunkel and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.
