items.content: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future — Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI Julian Kunkel Affiliation: Universität Göttingen, GWDG Email: julian.kunkel@gwdg.de Ali Doosthosseini Affiliation: Universität Göttingen Email: ali.doosthosseini@uni-goettingen.de November 5, 2026 Abstract Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access—giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface. Keywords: LLM chat interfaces, AI-era interfaces, meta access, application metamodels, interface agents, conversational search, feature tutoring, personas, guardrails, tool use, human–computer interaction, accessibility, local-first software. 1 Introduction The chat interface has been the default surface for interacting with large language models, and it remains the most common one for many day-to-day tasks: drafting, search, planning, learning, and personal assistance. In parallel, a second interaction model has matured. Agentic tools such as OpenCode [ 17 ] operate in a terminal or editor, call tools, and carry out multi-step tasks on external environments; they have become a natural choice for much software work. The two models are complementary rather than substitutes. Agents excel when the task is to operate on an environment, while chat UIs remain the natural surface when the user wants to ask, compare, plan, draft, or re-find something, and when the conversation itself is the workspace. The deeper claim of this paper is architectural rather than conversational. Chat is the first surface on which meta access is practical, but the pattern is not specific to chat. An emerging AI-era interface is one in which an assistant is embedded in the application rather than confined to a separate chat window, and in which the assistant can reason over the application’s own model of its state and capabilities. Whether the surface is a chat client, an IDE, a spreadsheet, a dashboard, or an operating system, the same asymmetry appears: the assistant sees the current task but not the workspace that contains it. Meta access is the missing contract between the two. The contrast is sharpest for general-purpose agentic harnesses such as OpenCode, which are runtimes rather than applications with a fixed purpose, and which can change the configuration that governs their own tools and permissions (Section 4.6 ). In applications such as Chat AI [ 7 ] , that workspace is larger than the current conversation: a sidebar of past conversations, user-defined topics, model selection, attachments, memories, settings, a persona library, and feature-specific controls. The model, however, usually sees only the current conversation plus a system prompt. Everything that makes the workspace a workspace—what else the user has discussed, how their chats are organised, which features exist and where they live—is outside the model’s view. This asymmetry creates a practical problem. As a user’s history grows, the interface becomes harder to navigate: finding a conversation about a past decision, remembering which topic contains it, or learning a rarely used feature requires manual scanning. Conventional search helps with known-item retrieval, but users often ask questions that are relational or procedural: “Where is my food-order chat?” , “Which topic holds the notes from the interview?” , “How do I attach a file?” . These are questions about the interface and its contents, not about the world. We use the term meta access for an assistant’s structured access to the interface that hosts it: it may access and potentially alter information about the interface and any of the user’s data. Meta access is related to, but distinct from, retrieval-augmented generation over documents [ 13 ] and tool use by language models [ 31 , 24 ] . The object of retrieval is the user’s own workspace state; the object of action is the interface itself. Meta access therefore sits at the intersection of conversational search, command palettes, recommender-style navigation, and agentic tool use. 1.1 What “meta” means here The prefix meta comes from Greek and denotes a level that is about, beyond, or refers to another level. Metadata is data about data; a metamodel is a model that describes the concepts and relations of another model; metacommunication is communication about communication. In each case, the meta-level does not replace the object level. It describes it, constrains it, or acts on it. A chatbot normally operates at the object level: it talks about the user’s task, the world, or the content of the current conversation. Meta access adds a meta-level whose object is the chat application itself. The assistant reasons about conversations, topics, memories, features, and settings rather than only about the subject of the dialogue. Its context is not the full interface but a workspace model: a structured description of the entities the interface exposes (chats, topics, features, preferences), ideally derived from the application’s own metamodel, and, eventually, the operations that can be requested on them. This is the sense in which the prototype has a metamodel-like view. It does not reproduce the interface; it uses an abstraction of the interface’s concepts and capabilities. At the scale of a whole application, this abstraction is an application metamodel: a description of the application’s entities, relations, and operations. Many applications already have such a model internally—a document model in an editor, a project and syntax model in an IDE, a schema in a database, a scene graph in a graphics tool—and debugging or profiling interfaces already expose parts of it in a controlled way. Meta access can reuse these models rather than relying on pixels or ad hoc scraping. The design question is which parts of the metamodel to expose, at what level of stability and permission, and how to map them into a capability layer that works across applications. The distinction separates three things that are easy to confuse. Metadata access is the narrowest form of meta access: it reads descriptive fields such as titles, topics, and timestamps. Meta-level knowledge also includes the feature catalogue, the persona catalogue, and current preference values, which describe the application rather than a single conversation. Meta-level action goes further and changes the object level, for example by moving a chat or changing a memory setting. The ladder in Section 4 follows this progression from describing the interface, to reading its state, to acting on it. We use “meta” in this self-referential sense, not in the corporate sense of Meta Platforms and not as a synonym for the metaverse. It is also different from meta-learning or meta-prompting: those describe learning or prompting about learning or prompting, whereas meta access describes an assistant’s access to the application that hosts the interaction. 1.2 Contributions This paper is a position paper grounded in an existing implementation. We make five contributions: 1. We present a ladder of meta-access levels that separates feature tutoring, metadata, settings, and preference access, summary and message-level retrieval, confirmed mutating actions, and full orchestration, and report how far the implemented prototype reaches on that ladder. 2. We propose meta access as a general design requirement for AI-era interfaces, not only chat clients, and show how the ladder, capability model, and guardrails transfer to other stateful applications and to general-purpose agentic harnesses, whose self-configuration adds a separate control-plane problem. 3. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access—giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface. In parallel, a second interaction model has matured. Agentic tools such as OpenCode [ 17 ] operate in a terminal or editor, call tools, and carry out multi-step tasks on external environments; they have become a natural choice for much software work. The two models are complementary rather than substitutes. Agents excel when the task is to operate on an environment, while chat UIs remain the natural surface when the user wants to ask, compare, plan, draft, or re-find something, and when the conversation itself is the workspace. The deeper claim of this paper is architectural rather than conversational. Chat is the first surface on which meta access is practical, but the pattern is not specific to chat. An emerging AI-era interface is one in which an assistant is embedded in the application rather than confined to a separate chat window, and in which the assistant can reason over the application’s own model of its state and capabilities. Whether the surface is a chat client, an IDE, a spreadsheet, a dashboard, or an operating system, the same asymmetry appears: the assistant sees the current task but not the workspace that contains it. Meta access is the missing contract between the two. The contrast is sharpest for general-purpose agentic harnesses such as OpenCode, which are runtimes rather than applications with a fixed purpose, and which can change the configuration that governs their own tools and permissions (Section 4.6 ). In applications such as Chat AI [ 7 ] , that workspace is larger than the current conversation: a sidebar of past conversations, user-defined topics, model selection, attachments, memories, settings, a persona library, and feature-specific controls. The model, however, usually sees only the current conversation plus a system prompt. Everything that makes the workspace a workspace—what else the user has discussed, how their chats are organised, which features exist and where they live—is outside the model’s view. This asymmetry creates a practical problem. As a user’s history grows, the interface becomes harder to navigate: finding a conversation about a past decision, remembering which topic contains it, or learning a rarely used feature requires manual scanning. Conventional search helps with known-item retrieval, but users often ask questions that are relational or procedural: “Where is my food-order chat?” , “Which topic holds the notes from the interview?” , “How do I attach a file?” . These are questions about the interface and its contents, not about the world. We use the term meta access for an assistant’s structured access to the interface that hosts it: it may access and potentially alter information about the interface and any of the user’s data. Meta access is related to, but distinct from, retrieval-augmented generation over documents [ 13 ] and tool use by language models [ 31 , 24 ] . The object of retrieval is the user’s own workspace state; the object of action is the interface itself. Meta access therefore sits at the intersection of conversational search, command palettes, recommender-style navigation, and agentic tool use. 1.1 What “meta” means here The prefix meta comes from Greek and denotes a level that is about, beyond, or refers to another level. Metadata is data about data; a metamodel is a model that describes the concepts and relations of another model; metacommunication is communication about communication. In each case, the meta-level does not replace the object level. It describes it, constrains it, or acts on it. A chatbot normally operates at the object level: it talks about the user’s task, the world, or the content of the current conversation. Meta access adds a meta-level whose object is the chat application itself. The assistant reasons about conversations, topics, memories, features, and settings rather than only about the subject of the dialogue. Its context is not the full interface but a workspace model: a structured description of the entities the interface exposes (chats, topics, features, preferences), ideally derived from the application’s own metamodel, and, eventually, the operations that can be requested on them. At the scale of a whole application, this abstraction is an application metamodel: a description of the application’s entities, relations, and operations. Ratings describe scope, not quality. This work implements selective message-level content retrieval and confirmed, reversible actions; the user-study column remains out of scope. Three patterns stand out. First, conversational search and PIM occupy opposite corners: conversational search supports dialogue and content retrieval but not the user’s personal workspace, while PIM supports personal metadata and content but not dialogue or interface actions. Second, agent and GUI-automation work supports actions and interface operation, but its object is an open environment rather than the user’s own conversation history; personal scope, structured workspace metadata, and user-facing grounding are typically absent. Third, memory and long-context work supports dialogue and personal context, but it rarely models the interface or provides a capability layer for acting on it. A trade-off is also visible: many systems that act do not expose citations to the underlying workspace items, while systems with strong grounding often do not act. Security work supplies adversarial benchmarks and defences but is rarely integrated with personal retrieval or interface help, and HCI work supplies interaction principles but not a concrete architecture. Meta access is the region that remains sparsely populated: personal scope, structured metadata, interface awareness, and grounding. Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 06, 2026 Back to Top

Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 06, 2026 Back to Top
